# 1\. Purpose & Scope  {#1.-purpose-&-scope}

![][image1]  
**Fig 1.0**: The software development cycle

This document will highlight the tech stack, architecture, environment, and best practices that is used for production. It will also highlight the common pitfalls when engineering an app and pushing to production. This document is the culmination of the problems we faced, the lessons we learnt, and the things we did right when building an application.

It will also roughly encompass nearly **all aspects of the SDLC** except analysis and UI/UX Design. While this document provides detailed guidance on implementation, testing, and deployment, the SDLC overview helps contextualise how all these practices fit together in a full software lifecycle.

As you scroll down, this document will gradually become more detailed, progressing from a high-level overview of the system architecture to increasingly specific implementation details, ultimately reaching the code-level design, optimizations and security aspects. This structure is intended to provide clear context before introducing technical complexity. However, this document requires a certain level of technical competency from the reader.

Do note that the contents of this document may change over time, and it is not required, though recommended, for legacy or ‘unconventional’ apps to follow strictly what is mentioned here. Ensuring robust knowledge management is imperative; this document serves that exact purpose.

# 2\. Tech Stack & Architecture For Standard Web Applications {#2.-tech-stack-&-architecture-for-standard-web-applications}

## **Overview** {#overview}

**Backend \- Python (Fast API)**  
**Frontend \- TypeScript (React)**  
**Authentication \- Keycloak**  
**Database \- Postgres**  
**Object Storage \- S3**  
**Infra (build) \- OpenShift, Helm Charts, ArgoCD, Github Actions (For development)**  
**Security \-  Trivy, SonarQube**  
**Code Quality \- Black, Flake8, ESLint, Prettier, SonarLint/SonarQube (npm/pip package \+ VSC Plugin), Extension config \+ linter config files**  
**Other tools \- [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/download), [Docker](https://www.docker.com/get-started/), [Git](https://git-scm.com/install/), [PgAdmin](https://www.pgadmin.org/download/), [Postman](https://www.postman.com/downloads/), Github Desktop ,Swagger, Figma**

### **Tech Stack Philosophy 理念** {#tech-stack-philosophy-理念}

As of now, the current tech stack is subject to change depending on whether the production environment changes its Managed Services, such as Authentication, Object Storage, Database and Load Balancing. This tech stack is specifically curated to have **seamless integration with production**. It was also chosen for its developer **ergonomics over speed, prioritising maintainability, readability, and ease of onboarding new team members.**

Languages such as Rust or Go may offer superior speed and robustness. However, this also entails a steeper learning curve and a more challenging developer experience as compared to Python or Ruby On Rails, especially in cases where such low level control is not strictly necessary. Hence for every project, the performance requirements would have to be considered thoroughly to determine the language to use, and also the level of code optimization required. 

A more ‘enterprise stack’ emphasises robustness and speed, it requires developers to invest more time upfront to understand and properly implement features, which may not always be justified for smaller-scale projects or prototypes.

### **Recommended Basic Architecture** {#recommended-basic-architecture}

This is the highly recommended architecture for web applications, where the containers/systems outside the dotted line are managed as production services**.** 

**To test the managed services in your development environment, download the local versions of the managed services** (will be provided later below in the document). Do keep in mind that local versions **may not be the same as production, depending on your setup**. 

For example, you do **not need to mount an SSL cert for development environments in managed services,** which is **mandatory in production environments**. There will be errors in production if you do not provide an SSL cert to the managed service.

**![][image2]**

### **Versioning** {#versioning}

Application released should follow the current best followed practice. 

### **Extending The Architecture** {#extending-the-architecture}

![][image3]

This document covers the core technologies used in the stack \- the database, frontend, and backend. If your application requires additional services such as **Redis, AI inference APIs, third-party APIs, or microservices**, you may extend the architecture to accommodate them. These can be connected directly using connection strings where appropriate, o**r through a front-facing API if the service needs to be consumed by multiple other services.**

**Whichever approach is chosen, it is strongly recommended to wrap the integration in an adapter in the backend**. As covered in the architecture section, adapters keep external service details \- connection logic, request formats, authentication \- contained in one place. If the service changes or is swapped out entirely, only the adapter needs to change, and the rest of the application is unaffected.

Refer to the [adapter architecture section here](#data-layer---adapter) 

### **Other Architectures & Modifying The Recommended Architecture**  {#other-architectures-&-modifying-the-recommended-architecture}

![][image4]

The recommended architecture is a starting point, not a strict constraint. Depending on your application's needs, the placement and ownership of services may differ from what is shown above.

A common variation is when services such as object storage or the database are not accessed directly by your backend, but are instead managed by separate internal APIs that your team owns. Rather than your backend connecting to PostgreSQL or S3 directly, it calls an internal API \- a Data API or a Storage API \- which handles the underlying interaction on your behalf. This is typical when those services are shared across multiple applications, and centralising access through a dedicated API makes more sense than each application managing its own connection and credentials.

From an adapter perspective, the approach is identical in both cases. Your backend still wraps every interaction in an adapter \- the only difference is what the adapter points at. In the recommended architecture it points directly at the service; in the modified architecture it points at the internal API instead. The rest of your application remains completely unaware of which arrangement is in place, which is precisely why the adapter pattern is valuable here.

**Framework Consistency across internal APIs** 

**![][image5]**

If possible, other internal APIs should follow the same technologies used in this stack. For example, if the main application does not own the database directly and instead calls an internal Data API, that internal API should still use SQLAlchemy as its database interactor and follow the same repository and adapter patterns described in this document.

This matters for two reasons. First, it reduces cognitive overhead \- a developer working across multiple services in the same team encounters the same patterns, the same exception types, and the same project structure regardless of which service they are in. Second, it makes it easier to move developers between services and to share code where appropriate, such as common exception classes or shared Pydantic models that describe the API contract between services.

Where deviating from the standard stack is necessary \- for example, if an internal API is owned by a different team or built in a different language \- the adapter in your backend absorbs that difference. The rest of your application remains unaffected, which is the entire point of the adapter boundary.

## **Backend** {#backend}

* **Programming Language**: Python 3.13 \- Subject to the latest stable version/Age of project  
* **Type Hint Module:** Python hints  
* **Virtual Environment:** Use .venv （For development)  
* **API Framework**: FastAPI \+ Uvicorn  
* **API Request & Type Validator:** Pydantic  
* **Object Relational Mapper**: SQLAlchemy 2.x   
* **ORM \+ API Integrator:** FastAPI-SQLAlchemy  
* **Database Driver:** psycopg (v3)  
* **Schema Migrator**: Alembic  
* **Authentication Adapter:** python-keycloak  
* **Object Storage Adapter:** Boto3  
* **Logger:** logging  
* **Testing:** unittest \+ pytest  
* **Other recommended non-core libraries: JWT**

### **Responsibilities of the Backend** {#responsibilities-of-the-backend}

* Act as the source of truth for all data **except user-related data and object storage images themselves**  
* Owns all business logic and validation rules (**Business logic should NOT be on the frontend**)  
  *(e.g., permission checks, state transitions, data validation, and invariants are enforced exclusively by the backend; the frontend performs UI-only validation)*  
* Sole interactor of the database (reads and writes)  
* Sole modifier of object storage  
* The sole interface grants administrator permissions in Keycloak.  
* Sole ‘receiver’ of data requests from the frontend  
* **Ensure that its own api can only be accessed using the Keycloak Token**

### 

### Programming Language {#programming-language}

The examples in this guide would mostly be in Python, with JavaScript and Rust for web development and C/C++ for general miscellaneous examples. The design principles can be brought across coding languages. Python is highly recommended for several reasons. As developers learn Python, it is easier to onboard them onto the project, which is also amplified by Python being an easy language to use due to its syntactic sugar and low verbosity. Python boasts a rich ecosystem of AI and data libraries, making it straightforward to manipulate data and integrate AI into the backend in addition to established API frameworks such as Flask and FastAPI.

 [Download Python Install Manager (3.13)](https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-31312/)

### Type Hint Module {#type-hint-module}

As Python is a dynamically typed language, it is hard to keep track of the types in which variables, functions or class constructor accepts. In order to reduce the burden of developers and runtime errors stemming from invalid types, developers should use python type hints. Type checking using `assert` can ensure clearer error messages and code readability.

[More About Typing & Tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html)

### Virtual Environment {#virtual-environment}

Each language has its own way of handling environments. Python uses a package manager such as pip that installs python code from a source archive. Languages that use package managers usually have a default archive that contains the dependency.

Using a virtual environment (venv) is highly recommended as it keeps dependencies project-specific. This avoids version conflicts between projects. This is especially helpful for developers who are working on multiple projects containing development environments..

#### Python {#python}

A concrete example of why `venv` is useful involves two projects with conflicting dependencies. Project A requires `fastapi==0.95` and `pydantic==1.x`, while Project B requires `fastapi==0.110` and `pydantic==2.x`. If you install all packages globally using `pip install fastapi pydantic`, one of the projects will inevitably break because the FastAPI versions depend on different Pydantic versions. 

##### Creating a Python venv {#creating-a-python-venv}

Through terminal: \``` /path/to/python -m venv .venv` ``

Using [virtualenv](https://pypi.org/project/virtualenv/): \``` virtualenv .venv --python=3.XX` ``

##### Activating a Python venv {#activating-a-python-venv}

There are a few basic methods to install a venv for your Python projects. Note that the packages in the venv might not be compatible with other python versions

Activating through VSCode UI: [Tutorial to Activate venv](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PQtlLzDiQF8)

#### C/C++ {#c/c++}

We will be using [Conan](https://conan.io/) as our package manager with source version control. Conan only works with precompiled libraries, so \`[`cmake`](https://cmake.org/download/)\` is required to build those libraries. The actual process would be out of scope for this bible, but here are some resources on how to use Conan:

Video: [Introduction to Conan](https://youtu.be/U-_RbUqDSTc)

Documentation: [Conan](https://docs.conan.io/2/)

### API Framework {#api-framework}

#### Python {#python-1}

FastAPI is the preferred choice for backend APIs due to its modern design, superior performance, and ease of use. Additional benefits include automatic data validation, built-in asynchronous support for high-concurrency applications, automatic OpenAPI/Swagger documentation, and strong type safety through Python type hints, reducing runtime errors. Despite all the benefits**, it is just as easy to use as Flask and boasts a very strong community ecosystem.**

[FastAPI Fundamentals Tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iWS9ogMPOI0) (With Pydantic Important\!)

[FastAPI Tutorial \+ Integration with SQLAlchem With Database](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xq1Snezb1rs) (Watch after watching the rest) (Highly recommended to know SQLAlchemy \+ FastAPI \+ Pydantic \- More in-depth)

[Fast API \+ React Integration](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aSdVU9-SxH4) (To understand how to make requests and responses with the backend and frontend)

### API Request Validator  & Type Validator {#api-request-validator-&-type-validator}

Pydantic is a data validation and parsing library based on Python type hints.

You define data models for your API Framework in the route (In this case, FastAPI) using normal Python types and Pydantic:

* Validates incoming data  
* Converts types automatically  
* Rejects invalid data with clear errors  
* Gives you strongly-typed objects to work with

This ensures fewer errors, as you have a guarantee that the incoming data is what you expect. It automatically checks missing attributes, and if it’s missing or incomplete, it will reject the incoming request.

[Pydantic Tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XIdQ6gO3Anc)

### Database Driver {#database-driver}

To interact with **Postgres** in the first place, you need to install **psycopg**. While SQLAlchemy translates objects to SQL queries, psycopg is the interface that talks to the Postgres database. Without it, we (by extension, SQLAlchemy) cannot communicate queries through Python. You do not need to do anything with it. SQLAlchemy will use psycopg internally.

[Psycopg](https://pypi.org/project/psycopg2-binary/)

### Object Relational Mapper {#object-relational-mapper}

SQLAlchemy is recommended over raw SQL queries because it reduces the risk of SQL injection and provides a higher-level, Pythonic interface for database operations. It also offers benefits such as:

* **Abstraction:** Work with Python objects instead of writing raw SQL.

* **Portability:** Easily switch between different database engines without changing your code.

* **Maintainability:** Cleaner, more readable, and reusable code.

* **Relationship Management:** Simplifies handling complex relationships between tables.

* **Query Flexibility:** Supports both high-level ORM queries and low-level SQL expressions when needed.

[SQLAlchemy Fundamentals](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xr7vDSFXjW0) 

[SQLAlchemy Fundamental Deep Dive](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6aD024WZfCs&t=687s) (Vtuber Ver)

### ORM \+ API Framework Integrator {#orm-+-api-framework-integrator}

To make integration with the ORM and the framework seamless, such as prepopulating the database, you should use FastAPI-SQLAlchemy. There is no need to control the lifecycle of the object as it is a Singleton and will handle memory and connection management for you. There is also no need to use Dependency Injection. 

[FastAPI-SQLAlchemy](https://pypi.org/project/FastAPI-SQLAlchemy/)

### Schema Migrator  {#schema-migrator}

Alembic is vital for easy migrations, particularly in production, where deleting and rebuilding the database from scratch is not an option, unlike in development environments. It allows developers to safely apply schema changes, track migration history, and maintain data integrity without downtime, ensuring that the application evolves smoothly as new features are added. For example, if you add a new table, you can use **Alembic to migrate to the latest schema in production.**

**For simple database migrations, use the autogenerate feature; it is much more convenient**

[Alembic with SQLAlchemy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i9RX03zFDHU&t=1363s)

### Authentication Adapter  {#authentication-adapter}

Python-keycloak should be used to interact with Keycloak. As a guideline, **this should only be used when you need to use a confidential client (Keycloak Admin API)**. For similar reasons as using keycloak-js, python-keycloak provides convenient and secure methods to interact with keycloak out-of-the-box without needing to manage a bunch of requests, reducing boilerplate code and improving readability. 

[Install Python Keycloak \+ Snippets](https://pypi.org/project/python-keycloak/) 

### Object Storage Adapter  {#object-storage-adapter}

Boto3 is the most widely used object storage library in Python. It provides a simple and consistent interface for interacting with AWS services such as S3 and local clients, enabling operations like uploading, downloading, and managing objects and buckets, all with one function. Beyond AWS, Boto3 can also be used with other compatible local object storage solutions, such as FlashBlade or MinIO, allowing developers to write storage-agnostic code.

[Boto3 \+ AWS Tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5q7FtT_DyME)

### Logger {#logger}

We should use the native python logging module. Compared to print, it enables us to create a flexible event logging system for our applications. Another benefit is that it allows us to categorise and type different logs such as errors, warning, and infos. It also allows us to further label and add additional supplementary data, allowing us to have a rich logging system. 

[Logging Tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/logging.html)

[More about logging](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html)

### Testing {#testing}

**pytest** is used as the test runnet and it handles test discovery, fixtures, and assertions.  
**unittest.mock** is used strictly for mocking and it replaces external dependencies such as repositories and S3 clients with controlled test doubles.

This separation allows tests to focus purely on business logic, keeping them fast, isolated, and independent of databases or network calls.

## **Frontend** {#frontend}

* **Programming Language:** TypeScript (6+)  
* **Build Tool:** Vite  
* **UI Framework**: React 19  
* **UI Navigation:** React Router  
* **HTTP Client**: Axios  
* **Client-Side Data Fetcher & State Manager**: TanStack Query  
* **Component Library:** ShadCN  
* **Style Library**: TailwindCSS  
* **Authentication Adapter:** Keycloak-js  
* **Testing:** Vitest

### **Responsibilities of the Frontend** {#responsibilities-of-the-frontend}

* Presents the user interface and user experience.  
* Collects user input and sends requests to the backend API along with the **keycloak token**.  
* Performs UI-only validation (e.g., required fields, input formatting, basic client-side feedback).  
* Renders backend responses and error states.  
* Does not contain business logic or authorisation decisions.  
* Does not directly access the database, modify object storage, or Keycloak administrative APIs  
* Only interact with Keycloak for login and retrieval of tokens  
* Only calls get requests using **only Presigned URLs to the object storage**

### Programming Language  {#programming-language-1}

TypeScript was chosen because it is similar to Python yet widely used in frontends across the web. It is also the de facto and main language used in React, with a very strong ecosystem and support. This makes it easy to onboard new people onto the project, reducing project friction. The language is also strongly typed, reducing the need to constantly check for correct types and runtime errors unlike JavaScript

### Build Tool {#build-tool}

Instead of Create React App, **Vite** should be used as a build tool. Vite is a modern development and build tool that emphasizes speed and efficiency. It provides fast hot module replacement (HMR), optimized bundling, and smooth development workflows. Compared to Create React App (CRA), it is much more reliable and updates faster upon a code change. 

\*Based on the author's experience, CRA can take up to 20 seconds to build and run the app, while VITE is at most 2 seconds.

### UI Framework {#ui-framework}

React is a widely used, component-based frontend library that allows building dynamic, interactive, and responsive user interfaces. Due to its state-first approach, managing JSON data that comes from the backend is easier to express through React. React also has a robust library ecosystem with extensive community support, making it easier for developers to find solutions, integrate third-party tools, accelerate development, and resolve errors. 

[Creating A React App](https://react.dev/learn/creating-a-react-app)

[React tutorial \- Fundamentals](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SqcY0GlETPk)

### UI Navigation {#ui-navigation}

React Router should be used for navigation because it integrates seamlessly with React. Since React is treated as a single-page application (SPA) in this architecture, navigation does not behave like traditional multi-page websites, where the navigation is simple enough to be handled by the browser itself, e.g clicking a link does not reload the page. React Router enables dynamic routing within the SPA, allowing developers to render different components based on the URL, manage nested routes, and maintain browser history, **all without full page reloads.** 

**Without navigation, if you reload the page, the current page you are on will not save, and it will go back to the home page.**

[React Router tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oTIJunBa6MA)

### HTTP Client {#http-client}

Axios is a promise-based HTTP client that simplifies communication with backend APIs, **particularly when you query data from the backend**. It provides a straightforward API for sending requests and handling responses, supports request/response interceptors, automatic JSON parsing, and easy configuration of authentication headers. Axios allows developers to efficiently manage API calls while keeping the code clean, compared to the native Fetch API.

[Here is one example of Axios vs Fetch](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/40844297/what-is-difference-between-axios-and-fetch)

### Component Library {#component-library}

Shadcn/ui is a collection of accessible, reusable components built on Radix UI primitives (components usch as toasts, date pickers, dropdown). Unlike traditional component libraries, it is not installed as a dependency \- components are copied directly into your codebase, giving you full ownership and control to customise them. Each component is unstyled by default and uses **Tailwind CSS** for styling, making it easy to adapt to any design system. ShadCN enables the team to have consistent components across multiple applications making it easier for developers and enables the team design to be established.

[ShadCN Tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yz3Rfn_UJOo)

### Style Library {#style-library}

Tailwind CSS is a utility-first CSS framework that lets you style elements directly in your markup using small, composable class names. Instead of writing custom CSS, you apply pre-defined utilities like flex, p-4, or text-sm directly to your components. This approach keeps styles co-located with markup, eliminates unused CSS automatically, and makes it easy to build consistent UIs without leaving your HTML or JSX.

### Client State Fetcher & State Manager {#client-state-fetcher-&-state-manager}

TanStack Query is a powerful library for handling asynchronous data fetching, caching, and state management in React applications. It helps keep UI components clean by separating API interface logic from presentation, automatically handling loading, errors, and cache updates. It is a replacement for UseEffect where you have to manually initalise and manage state. It is the bridge for data (request and responses) between the React world and the API World.

Particularly when using Keycloak, one should use the keycloak-js library to interact with Keycloak. **Instead of managing access tokens and refresh tokens manually with LocalStorage or SessionStorage, keycloak-js handles token management and user redirection automatically.** It also provides out-of-the-box functionality, such as retrieving user information without manually decoding JWT tokens. Additionally, **keycloak-js simplifies implementing features like role-based access control,** token expiration handling, silent token refresh, and single sign-on (SSO) across multiple applications, reducing boilerplate code and ensuring secure, standardised authentication workflows.

Keycloak-js can reduce boilerplate code from a few hundred lines down to only dozens of lines.

## **Keycloak** {#keycloak}

**F[rontend code implementation refer to here](#authentication-architecture)**

**B[ackend code implementation refer to here](#architecturing-your-classes-and-components)**

* **IdP (Identity Provider)**: Keycloak  
* **Realm:** One realm (Assume ANYBODY can access the realm)  
* **Groups:** Min. one group per application  
* **Backend Client:** Use Confidential Client (only if the backend needs to interact directly with Keycloak)  
* **Frontend Client:** Use Public Client  
* **Roles: Separate with Admin/User Roles  & ONLY USE client roles**   
* **Redirect:** Only necessary links such as your application endpoints  
* **SSL: Recommended for development |** Required for production environments  
* **Custom Attributes:** If needed

[**Install Keycloak**](https://www.keycloak.org/getting-started/getting-started-zip)

[**Tutorial For Keycloak (Realm, Confidential Clients, Public Clients)**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fvxQ8bW0vO8)

**Related library to interact with Keycloak: [Python Keycloak,](#authentication-adapter) \+  [Keycloak JS](#authentication-adapter-1)**

### Naming Conventions {#naming-conventions}

**Realm:** yourprojectname-realm

**Group:** yourprojectname-app-nameofgroup

**Backend Client:** yourprojectname-backend-client

**Frontend Client:** yourprojectname-frontend-client

**Roles:** yourprojectname-nameofyourrole

The naming convention for all clients, realms and roles should be skewer \+ all lowercase with your project's name at the start of the name. This ensures that if developers jump from one project to another they have an easier time onboarding and context switching, accelerating development. 

### About Keycloak {#about-keycloak}

Keycloak is an open-source Identity and Access Management solution that provides authentication, authorisation, and user management for applications. It’s an identity provider that handles login, logout, and token management in a secure manner. **Because applications in the production environment can be accessed by anybody**, it is **important to secure your entire application using Keycloak and enforce mandatory login upon visiting the website.** 

Keycloak is chosen as an IdP because it is the de facto authentication provider for production. In order to push into production with less friction, Keycloak is sacrosanct. **Keycloak uses JWT** as the mechanism for communicating identity and claims between the IdP and your application

You can install the local version of Keycloak to test in your development environment here: [OpenJDK \- Keycloak](https://www.keycloak.org/getting-started/getting-started-zip).

![][image6]

### How is Keycloak Managed in Production {#how-is-keycloak-managed-in-production}

In production, Keycloak is a shared platform administered by the platform team \- not by individual application teams. A single **realm** hosts all applications in the environment, each registered as a separate **client**. Your application is one tenant among many, and you have no control over users, realm configuration, or how other clients are set up.

Users are pre-provisioned. They are synced from LDAP or Active Directory, or created directly by platform admins. Your application never creates, modifies, or deletes users \- it only reads what the JWT token tells you about whoever has logged in.

![][image7]

Because a user existing in the realm doesn't mean they have access to *your* app, access is gated by **group membership**. Each application has a designated group; if a user isn't in it, they're turned away. Your backend should enforce this by inspecting the `groups` claim in the JWT \- absent or mismatched, the session is rejected before anything else runs (through the code).

Once inside, what a user can actually do is controlled by **client roles** \- roles scoped specifically to your application's client ID. These appear in the token under `resource_access.<your-client-id>.roles`, and are what your backend checks when protecting individual routes or actions. Because they're scoped to your client, they don't bleed into other apps sharing the same realm.

This gives three distinct layers to reason about, each with a clear owner:

![][image8]

Keycloak owns layer 1 \- it's configured by the platform team and you interact with its output (the token), not its internals. Your application owns layers 2 and 3\. In development, you'll simulate all of this yourself using a local Keycloak instance, but the token structure is identical to production, so the code you write translates directly.

### Keycloak Token-Based Auth Architecture Flow/Stack {#keycloak-token-based-auth-architecture-flow/stack}

**Note that the tokens mentioned here are JWT Tokens because they are used in Keycloak.** This part is used to show the set of related components, tools and flows used to handle authentication and authorisation in the application. 

Where:  
**Keycloak** \- Identity provider issuing tokens  
**Frontend** \- Obtains tokens and attaches it to requests **(This is where your Public Client is used)**  
**Backend** \- Verifies tokens, enforces roles/permissions, and accepts the request if the token is valid **(You do not need a Confidential Client for these operations)**

**Request Handshake between frontend, backend and keycloak**

**![][image9]**

Login is not handled by your application. When an unauthenticated user visits the app, the frontend redirects them to Keycloak's hosted login page. Your app never sees the user's credentials \- Keycloak handles the entire login interaction and, on success, redirects back to your app with tokens attached.

Keycloak issues two tokens: an access token, which is a short-lived JWT used to authenticate API requests, and a refresh token, which is longer-lived and used solely to obtain a new access token when the current one expires. The frontend stores both and is responsible for checking token expiry proactively \- before sending a request, not after receiving a 401\. keycloak-js handles this transparently if you initialise it with onTokenExpired. Otherwise, you could handle the access token refresh yourself by using timers like setInterval in TypeScript/Javascript.

![][image10]

For every subsequent API request, the frontend attaches the access token in the `Authorization` header as a Bearer token. The backend then validates it \- not by calling Keycloak on every request, but by verifying the token's signature using Keycloak's public key, which it fetches once on startup. Validation checks four things: the signature (was this issued by our Keycloak?), the issuer (`iss` claim), the expiry (`exp` claim), and the audience (`aud` claim, which should match your client ID). All four must pass. If the token is valid and the user has the required group membership and client roles, the backend returns the requested data. Otherwise it returns a `401` (invalid or expired token) or `403` (valid token, insufficient permissions).

**![][image11]**

The key practical point for developers: your backend never calls Keycloak per request. It validates the token locally using the public key. This means a revoked token can still pass validation until it expires \- which is why access tokens are kept short-lived (typically 5–15 minutes), and why the refresh token exists.

### Realm {#realm}

A realm in Keycloak secures and manages metadata for a set of users, applications, and registered OAuth clients. Their scope is typically used for **multiple applications where roles span across all applications**. A realm can contain **multiple clients, where the client can be a confidential client or a public client for a specific application**. Do note for production, **multiple applications are a tenant of one realm,** so you should keep to client scope roles and permissions**. This means that all users that are not part of your application, still can view your application if they are a user. If you want to prevent that, use GROUPS**. For development, you are free to use a specific realm per application.

### Groups {#groups}

Since a single production realm contains all users across all applications \- including external clients \- roles alone are not sufficient to restrict access to specific applications. You should use **Keycloak Groups** to organise users by the application(s) they are permitted to access or control.

* Assign users to groups that correspond to the applications they should have access to (e.g. `yourprojectname-app-users`, `yourprojectname-app-admins`)  
* Groups should be **included in the JWT token** via a mapper \- add a Group Membership mapper to your client so that group membership is passed in the token claims  
* The backend should then validate **both** the role (what the user can do) and the group (which app they belong to) on each request  
* Do not rely solely on roles for app-level access gating in a shared realm, as roles are visible and potentially applicable across all clients in the realm

### Frontend Client {#frontend-client}

Browser-based applications like React cannot store secrets safely \- anything bundled into the frontend is readable by anyone who inspects the page source or network traffic. **Public clients exist for exactly this reason**: they authenticate without a client secret, using an authorisation code flow called PKCE instead.

PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) protects against authorisation code interception. The flow works like this:

1. The frontend redirects the user to Keycloak's hosted login page.  
2. After successful authentication, Keycloak redirects back to the frontend with a short-lived, one-time authorisation code.  
3. The frontend exchanges that code for an access token and a refresh token by calling Keycloak's token endpoint.

**You do not need to implement any of this manually. `keycloak-js` handles the entire PKCE flow** when you initialise it \- including token storage, proactive refresh before expiry, and redirect handling. Once initialised, your only responsibility is to attach the access token to every API request sent to the backend.

### Backend Client {#backend-client}

In most cases, a frontend public client is sufficient \- the backend only needs the realm's public key to verify JWTs, which requires no client secret.

A backend confidential client is needed when the **backend itself** needs to **call Keycloak's endpoints directly**. This falls into two levels:

**Standard OIDC operations (Can be used in Production)**\- such as token exchange (password grant), token refresh, token introspection, and logout. These use Keycloak's OpenID Connect token endpoint and require the client secret to authenticate the request. This is a standard confidential OIDC client with no special permissions.

**Administrative operations (Only for Development Testing)** \- such as creating or deleting users, assigning roles, and reading realm configuration. These use the Keycloak Admin REST API and require the confidential client to have **Service Accounts enabled** with the appropriate realm-management roles assigned (e.g., `manage-users`, `view-users`). **You do not have administrative operations in Keycloak.**

Since the client secret never leaves the backend, these capabilities are inherently restricted to server-side code. This cannot be done through public clients.

You should use libraries such as **python-keycloak** for confidential clients in the backend, as it provides a high-level, secure interface for both standard OIDC flows and administrative tasks \- such as querying users, managing roles and groups, performing token introspection, and calling protected Keycloak endpoints \- without manually handling token requests, client secrets, or REST API calls.

**![][image12]**

### Roles {#roles}

If you require users to be split between different permissions, for example, admin and normal users, you should use roles. You will also need to **hide the UI from non-admin users and secure your backend by checking valid users and user roles. You can use keycloak-js to check for user roles, and you can decrypt using the JWT library in the backend to check the roles.**

The production environment only accepts **client roles,** and you should not use Realm roles. This is because multiple applications that are not related to your own application are also a part of a tenant in the realm. Do keep in mind that if you change from realm roles to client roles, there will be some code changes that are required due to the difference in where the roles are tracked in the JSON structure.


### Redirects {#redirects}

It is highly recommended to set only the destinations that you are going to redirect to and from. For example, from the frontend to Keycloak login and from Keycloak login back to the frontend. **You should not allow any other websites to redirect to your Keycloak login**, and Keycloak to redirect to other websites for security. 

### SSL {#ssl}

SSL is only required in production environments. However, it is best practice to run a mock or staging server that enforces SSL as well, to reduce the risk of environment-specific issues, catch misconfigurations early, and ensure your application behaves consistently under secure connections. **There is a difference not just in configuration but in code if you want to introduce certificates.**

[**Configure SSL on Keycloak**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WAgHhRgqkFM)

### Custom Attributes {#custom-attributes}

If you require additional data for users (e.g., birthday, family, etc.), **use Keycloak’s additional attributes. You should not maintain a separate custom database for user information**. At most, you may store the user ID in your backend to reference related data, but all personal attributes should remain in Keycloak.

### About Postgres {#about-postgres}

Postgres is an SQL database, and it’s chosen because it’s a managed service that is used in production. In order to reduce the friction between development environments and production environments, Postgres was chosen. **If you do need to use Postgres in production, you should not bring your own image of Postgres.** You should provision it from the production environment and use their credentials.

###  Other tools {#other-tools}

If you do need to inspect the database or query additional things from the database, you should use PgAdmin. It is quite easy to use, and it is easy to onboard. However, it is important to keep in mind that **learning SQL is also important since production does not have PgAdmin for you to inspect when debugging. The PSQL command line is available in the pod, so it is possible to inspect it through the command line.**

### Prepopulation Of Database {#prepopulation-of-database}

Prepopulation of the database is allowed only in Helm charts or done automatically in the application **and cannot be done manually in the production environment using a script of any kind**. You may use **SQLAlchemy** to build all the tables and prepopulate data using it on application startup. It is important, though, to check whether the data has been prepopulated already before doing the prepopulation of data.

[Prepopulate Database](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/56063458/pre-populate-a-flask-sqlalchemy-database) (Use SQLAlchemy \+ Use scope from SQLAlchemy-FastAPI)

[Prepopulation Gist Using FastAPI, SQLAlchemy-FastAPI, SQLAlchemy](https://gist.github.com/Ronandt/6c9a160a84d0f114b57bb553458b5822)

### Access {#access}

Only the backend should be able to access the database. No other entity is allowed to access the database. Hide secrets as much as possible and only backend should have the secrets.

### 

### Object Storage Provider {#object-storage-provider}

As ‘flashblade’ is unobtainable for development environments, there are a few other object storage clients that have the same standard/protocol where **Boto3** can interact with from the backend. Although Boto3 is mainly used to interact with AWS, due to the environment differences (e.g., non-local), it will create more friction between development and the production environment. There is also no way to use custom SSLs, as AWS will take care of that for you.

**Therefore, local clients such as Minio/GarageHQ are recommended for development as they enable the development environment to be closer to the production environment. They also allow you to enforce your custom SSL certificates.**

### Enable SSL {#enable-ssl}

SSL is required in production environments (will be given to you) to ensure secure communication and protect data in transit. **For development environments, local object storage clients like MinIO or GarageHQ allow you to enforce SSL, which helps mimic production behavior and catch configuration issues early. Enabling SSL in developmen**t ensures that certificate errors, connection issues, and secure communication behaviors are tested before deployment.

WIP (We are struggling to use SSL to connect to the managed services in production as of now)

### 

### Object GET Access {#object-get-access}

**![][image13]**

It is mandatory to use presigned URLs in both development and production environments. Without presigned URLs, anyone with the object link can access it at any time, bypassing access controls. However, with presigned URLs, the access is temporary and time-limited, and permissions are enforced for each request. This ensures that objects are only accessible to authorized users for a defined period, reducing the risk of unauthorized access or accidental exposure. The flow should work like this:

* The frontend requests data from the backend, including images for a certain use case.  
* The backend retrieves the presigned URL for each image from the object storage server **(Should use Boto3)** using the image’s name or ID (that comes from the database).  
* The backend responds to the frontend with the presigned URLs.  
* The frontend uses the presigned URLs to access the images securely and temporarily.

More information: [https://fourtheorem.com/the-illustrated-guide-to-s3-pre-signed-urls/](https://fourtheorem.com/the-illustrated-guide-to-s3-pre-signed-urls/)

It should be assumed that all public access is disabled for security, and the only way to obtain objects is through Presigned URLs. **This behavior is also seen in production, where bucket access is disabled. As a result, attempting to access an object via its link as if it were public will cause errors, and the object will not be displayed.**

### Bucket creation {#bucket-creation}

In production, there is no need to create a bucket, as they will create one for you, and you do not have permission to create one. Therefore, it is recommended that you **create the bucket manually, even in development, in the client instead of automatically in the application,** to reduce the amount of code change from development to production.

## Code Quality  {#code-quality}

[**Refer to Enforcing Code Quality Section to enforce linters and formatters**](#enforcing-linters-&-formatters-in-development-stage) 

* **Frontend Linter (VSC Plugin \+ NPM Package)**: EsLint  
* **Frontend Formatter (VSC Plugin \+ NPM Package):** Prettier  
* **Backend Linter (VSC Plugin \+ NPM Package):** Flake8  
* **Backend Formatter (VSC Plugin \+ NPM Package):** Black  
* **Static Analyser (Code Quality) (VSC Plugin):** SonarLint (In Text Editor)/SonarQube (CI/CD)


  
![][image15]

### About Plugins {#about-plugins}

Plugins (or extensions) are integrations for your code editor, such as VS Code, that allow the editor to interact with the underlying packages. They provide **real-time feedback**, such as highlighting syntax errors, code smells, formatting issues, and maintainability warnings, directly in the editor. Plugins do not perform the actual linting or formatting themselves. But instead, they act as a bridge between the editor and the installed package, making it easier for developers to see issues and automatically fix them while writing code. Examples include the ESLint and Prettier plugins for frontend development, the Python extension for running Flake8 or Black in VS Code, and SonarLint for code quality feedback.

### About Packages  {#about-packages}

Packages are the actual tools or “engines” that perform the work, such as linting, formatting, or static analysis. They are installed in your project or system \- usually via **npm** for frontend tools (like ESLint and Prettier) or **pip** for Python backend tools (like Flake8 and Black). Packages run in the terminal or as part of a CI/CD pipeline, and they ensure consistent code quality and formatting across different environments and developers. **While plugins integrate these packages into the editor for real-time feedback, the packages themselves are what actually perform the checks and transformations on the code.**

**Compared to Plugins, Packages are project based, meaning that the linting/formatting rules are baked into your project as opposed to having it locally,** enabling all developers working on the same project to follow the same rules. **It is also integratable with CI/CD as CI/CD can use these rules in the project to govern code quality**

### Frontend Linter {#frontend-linter}

ESLint is a tool for identifying and reporting on patterns in ECMAScript/TypeScript Code. It also supports JSX syntax allowing standards to be enforced in React code. You can configure ESLint’s built in rules based on the project to standardise the code across the project. 

Download: [https://eslint.org/](https://eslint.org/)

### Frontend formatter {#frontend-formatter}

Prettier is the most famous frontend formatter for HTML, CSS and JS, and JSX (React). It automatically formats the code based on the configuration, reducing the burden for developers as they do not have to consistently manually format code. Although the Linter can format code, Prettier is more opinionated.

For the backend, **Flake8** is used as the linter to enforce PEP8 coding standards and detect common issues such as unused imports, undefined variables, and stylistic inconsistencies.

Install SonarLint (Plugin): [https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=SonarSource.sonarlint-vscode](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=SonarSource.sonarlint-vscode)

## Security Tools {#security-tools}

* **Vulnerability Scanner:** Trivy  
* **Static Code Analyser:** SonarQube

### Vulnerability Scanner {#vulnerability-scanner}

Trivy scans container images, filesystems, and Git repositories for known security vulnerabilities. It focuses on finding issues in the OS packages, language dependencies, and container layers. **Trivy reports are required for production whenever you send a new container in.**

[https://trivy.dev/docs/latest/getting-started/](https://trivy.dev/docs/latest/getting-started/)

### Static Code Analyser {#static-code-analyser}

SonarQube analyses the entire application’s **source code for quality, bugs, security vulnerabilities, and code smells**. It works for multiple languages (Python, Java, JS/TS, Go, etc.). SonarQube reports are also **required for production.**

**It is recommended that you use this for your CI (GitHub Actions) to ensure code quality. You should use SonarLint for your text editor.**

Compared to SonarLint, SonarQube performs a **comprehensive analysis of the entire application**, rather than just the local files open in the IDE. This deeper scope allows it to detect **system-level issues, code duplication, architectural concerns, and security vulnerabilities** that may span multiple modules or services.

Because it analyses the full codebase and produces metrics and dashboards, it is inherently more resource-intensive and slower than local analysis which is why it should be used in CI (only when you merge).

[https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarqube/downloads/](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarqube/downloads/)
