# 3\. Different Developer Roles & Responsibilities  {#3.-different-developer-roles-&-responsibilities}

Based on the stack given, developer roles can be roughly divided into three roles. Although ideally, a full-stack developer should have the ability to do all three roles, the amount of technologies and tools one has to learn in a short amount of time, coupled with the short lifecycle of the average developer, in this case, it is unreasonable to expect a developer to know and learn all three unless they have prior experience.

If the developer has a certain level of competency, they may take up more than one role.

### Backend Developer Responsibilities  {#backend-developer-responsibilities}

A backend developer should be able to:

* Architecture of the backend APIs  
* Understand all the technologies listed in the **backend section** of the stack  
* Integrate APIs with mock managed services (Database, Keycloak, and S3 \- Object Storage)  
* Document the backend (E.g Swagger API) for frontend developers and DevOps engineers  
* Basic understanding of how the frontend works (How the frontend sends the request, how the backend responds, and how they integrate)  
* Liaise with the frontend developers on API needs  
* **Should know how env management works in production (Secrets.yaml \+ Values.yaml) and how it’s piped into the application**  
* **Liaise with the DevOps engineer to define, validate, and document all configuration values and secrets required by the application (critical for production), enabling accurate creation of `values.yaml` and `secrets.yaml`.**

### Frontend Developer Responsibilities {#frontend-developer-responsibilities}

A frontend developer should be able to:

* Understand UI/UX patterns and the users' requirements  
* Be able to use UI/UX design tools such as Figma and create high-fidelity prototypes for the client  
* Architecture of the frontend  
* Understand all the technologies listed in the **frontend section** of the stack  
* Liaise with the backend developers for API needs  
* Basic understanding of how the backend works (How the frontend sends the request, how the backend responds, and how they integrate). Be able to read documentation from the backend developer  
* **Should know how env management works in production (Secrets.yaml \+ Values.yaml) and how it’s piped into the application**  
* **Liaise with the DevOps engineer to define, validate, and document all configuration values and secrets required by the application (critical for production), enabling accurate creation of `values.yaml` and `secrets.yaml`.**

### DevOps Engineer Responsibilities  {#devops-engineer-responsibilities}

A DevOps engineer should be able to:

* Understand the entire overarching architecture of the application (Including how Docker containers and managed services are orchestrated, networked, and configured (e.g., connectivity, ports, and service dependencies))  
* Set up CI/CD Pipelines to ensure code quality  
* Generate and provide materials needed for deployment, such as Trivy Scans, Umbrella charts, and documentation, and RFO   
* Knowledge of Dockerisation   
* Set up Helm charts and be able to deploy on Kubernetes and OpenShift  
* Be able to set up all services, such as the Database, Keycloak, and S3, from scratch, and **configure the settings for the application (Secrets and Values) and configuration in managed services with the help of the backend developer and frontend developer**




Particularly for deployment, all parties need to work very closely with one another to ensure that there are no discrepancies when converting the development environment to a production-ready app. Ideally, there should be a pre-staging environment where all the managed services are set up in the same way as production, controlled by one server.

As a measure, after the DevOps engineer sets up the OpenShift environment, **all modifications in the architecture in development and all modifications of secret and configuration variables, including name changes, should be clearly notified by the frontend and backend developers to the DevOps engineer.** 

# 4\. Best Practices, Software Design Patterns, And Architecturing Your Code {#4.-best-practices,-software-design-patterns,-and-architecturing-your-code}

## The Overarching Clean Code Architecture & Best Practices {#the-overarching-clean-code-architecture-&-best-practices}

### Overview ![][image16] {#overview-1}

[Inspired by Google’s Mobile Architecture](https://developer.android.com/topic/architecture), the architecture is generalised into 3 layers (UI Layer/Presentation Layer, Domain Layer, and Data layer) where the frontend and backend share the responsibility for presentation, while business logic and data access remain strictly within the backend. 

The purpose of separating the layers is so that each layer serves a specific purpose, decoupling different functions so that if one layer changes, it doesn’t affect the other layer. Additionally, the layer below the layer above should not know about the specifics.

To elaborate, dependencies flow inward. The **Presentation Layer** interacts only with the **Domain Layer**, which contains business logic and calls the **Data Layer** through repository interfaces. The **Data Layer** implements these interfaces using the database or external services. No layer calls outward, so the UI never accesses the database directly, and the domain remains independent of frameworks or infrastructure.

The benefits of this include:

* Isolation of concerns (E.g changing from React to Svelte won’t affect the rest of the layers)  
* Testability (Ability to test business logic in isolation)  
* Maintainability (New features can be added without breaking unrelated parts)  
* Lesser bugs (Easier to track and fix bugs)

As you get further into this section, there will be more information about how to architect such that there are clear layers and responsibilities. 

**UI Layer**

* Handles interaction with the outside world.  
* Validates input and formats output.  
* Does not implement business logic or access the database directly.  
* Does not know the Data Layer

**Domain Layer**

* Contains the core business rules and workflows.  
* Orchestrates operations by using interfaces to the Data Layer.  
* Independent of frameworks, UI, and database technology.  
* Does not know the UI layer

**Data Layer**

* Manages persistence and access to external systems.  
* Source of truth of data  
* Shields domain and presentation layers from storage and infrastructure details  
* Does not know the Domain Layer

For reference on what architecture components should be categorised as:

          ![][image17]

### Overarching File Structure {#overarching-file-structure}

Your files should be structured in a way that is understandable and meaningful among developers.

**Top hierarchy**   
**.**  
**├── projectname-backend/**  
**│**  
**├── projectname-frontend/**  
**│**  
**├── projectname-submission/**  
**│**  
**├── .dockerignore**  
**│**  
**├── .gitignore**  
**│**  
**└── README.md**

Your top-level hierarchy should contain three folders, the other files required to build the entire application, and documentation for the entire application. There should not be any backend or frontend-specific folders, such as package.json, package-lock.json, and virtual environment. This hierarchy reflects the state of your application's needs and its own ecosystem. 

Your submissions folder should contain all the materials needed and required for RFO as well as production.

## Backend Clean Code Architecture {#backend-clean-code-architecture}

### **Backend Clean Architecture Overview** {#backend-clean-architecture-overview}

![][image18]

The backend is separated into three layers: the UI layer, the domain layer, and the data layer. Each layer has a defined responsibility, and the implementation of a higher layer must not leak into a lower one — the domain layer should have no knowledge of FastAPI request/response mechanics, and the data layer should have no knowledge of either.

This separation improves maintainability, testability, and long-term flexibility. Changes to how data is persisted should not require changes to business logic, and changes to API contracts should not require changes to the database schema.

![][image19]

Layers do not share a single common type across the whole stack. Instead, the domain layer acts as a translation boundary \- SQLAlchemy models are the currency between the data and domain layers, and Pydantic models are the currency between the domain and UI layers. The domain layer is the only layer that sees both, and is responsible for converting between them.

This split exists for technical reasons, not just architectural preference. SQLAlchemy models are tightly coupled to the database session \- they carry ORM machinery, lazy-load relationships on attribute access, and can trigger additional queries if accessed outside a session context. Passing them directly to a route handler or returning them in a response would mean FastAPI is serialising a live database object, which is fragile and unpredictable. Pydantic models, by contrast, are plain validated data \- no session, no lazy loading, no side effects. They serialise cleanly and describe exactly the shape of the data your API exposes.

The conversion is also not always mechanical. Returning a Pydantic model from the domain layer is often the point where business logic runs \- resolving a stored S3 object key into a fresh presigned URL, computing a derived field, or stripping fields the caller shouldn't see. Doing this in the domain layer keeps that logic out of both the repository (which should only care about persistence) and the route handler (which should only care about HTTP).

**As a rule of thumb: a layer may import *what* something is, but not *how* it is handled by another layer.**

---

#### When Your Application Does Not Own The DB Layer {#when-your-application-does-not-own-the-db-layer}

![][image20]

**Note:** The SQLAlchemy/Pydantic translation boundary described above applies when the backend owns its database directly via SQLAlchemy. If your architecture is modified such that the data layer calls an internal API instead of querying the database directly, this boundary shifts. The repository receives JSON from the internal API and parses it into a Pydantic model directly \- SQLAlchemy is no longer involved, and the domain layer never sees an ORM object. In this case the repository returns a Pydantic model, the domain layer receives a Pydantic model, and `_resolve` in the service may still exist for business logic like presigned URL generation, but it is no longer responsible for type conversion. The internal API itself becomes the translation boundary \- it owns the mapping from database rows to the JSON your backend consumes.

**Separate Application By Feature \- Vertical Slice Architecture**

![][image21]

With the exception of shared architectural components (infrastructure) such as adapters, utils and dependencies; **routers, repository, services, related DB models should be in one folder per use case** because they heavily depend on one another instead of separating by layers. 

This method is chosen because it works well for simpler applications, where business logic is largely self-contained and there is minimal cross-domain interaction. For example, if you were to separate by layers, you might need to go through several directories when implementing a feature. However, in vertical slice architecture, you would only need to navigate through the directory you’re working in.

This method follows the Common Closure Principle (CCP 🇨🇳) which states:

*“Classes within a component should be grouped together based on the same kind of changes they are susceptible to. When a change affects a component, it should impact all the classes within that component and no other components. ”*

Therefore, based on this principle, the code that is more reliant on another part of the codebase should be more coupled and closer to one another. In order to do that directories in the application should be split by feature which will be shown below.

### **Structuring the Backend Your Files** {#structuring-the-backend-your-files}

**Backend folder**  
As the name suggests, the backend folder should only contain backend-related code, builds, and libraries. Within the backend folder, there should be files such as

**architecture-project-backend/**  
**│**  
**├── app/**  
**│   ├── \_\_init\_\_.py**  
**│   │**  
**│   ├── main.py                        \# FastAPI app instance, middleware registration, startup events**  
**│   ├── .env                           \# Environment variables for development**  
**│   ├── example.env                    \# Example env file to be committed — never commit .env**  
**│   │**  
**│   ├── features/                      \# Feature-based modules**  
**│   │   │**  
**│   │   ├── users/**  
**│   │   │   ├── \_\_init\_\_.py**  
**│   │   │   ├── router.py              \# FastAPI routes for user-related endpoints**  
**│   │   │   ├── schemas.py             \# Pydantic request/response models for the Users API**  
**│   │   │   ├── model.py               \# SQLAlchemy User model**  
**│   │   │   ├── repository.py          \# Data access — user-specific queries and persistence**  
**│   │   │   ├── service.py             \# User business logic (uses repository and adapters)**  
**│   │   │   └── dependencies.py        \# FastAPI dependency providers scoped to Users**  
**│   │   │**  
**│   │   └── items/**  
**│   │       ├── \_\_init\_\_.py**  
**│   │       ├── router.py              \# FastAPI routes for item-related endpoints**  
**│   │       ├── schemas.py             \# Pydantic request/response models for the Items API**  
**│   │       ├── model.py               \# SQLAlchemy Item model**  
**│   │       ├── repository.py          \# Data access — item-specific queries and persistence**  
**│   │       ├── service.py             \# Item business logic (uses repository and adapters)**  
**│   │       └── dependencies.py        \# FastAPI dependency providers scoped to Items**  
**│   │**  
**│   ├── infrastructure/                \# External system integrations and app-level plumbing**  
**│   │   ├── \_\_init\_\_.py**  
**│   │   ├── database.py                \# SQLAlchemy engine and session factory**  
**│   │   ├── base.py                    \# SQLAlchemy declarative Base class**  
**│   │   ├── middleware.py              \# Global FastAPI middleware (use Depends instead where possible)**  
**│   │   ├── logging.py                 \# Logging configuration — called once at startup in main.py**  
**│   │   │**  
**│   │   └── adapters/                  \# Wrappers around external services (boto3, python-keycloak)**  
**│   │       ├── keycloak\_adapter.py    \# Keycloak integration**  
**│   │       └── s3\_adapter.py          \# S3 integration**  
**│   │**  
**│   └── shared/                        \# Cross-cutting code used by all layers**  
**│       ├── \_\_init\_\_.py**  
**│       ├── config.py                  \# Pydantic Settings — all env vars declared here, never read os.environ directly**  
**│       ├── dependencies.py            \# Shared FastAPI dependencies (auth, adapter singletons, DB session)**  
**│       ├── schemas.py                 \# Shared Pydantic models (TokenClaims, RoleAccess)**  
**│       ├── exceptions.py              \# Custom application exceptions with HTTP status codes**  
**│       └── utils/**  
**│           ├── \_\_init\_\_.py**  
**│           └── helpers.py             \# Shared utility functions**  
**│**  
**├── tests/**  
**│   ├── \_\_init\_\_.py**  
**│   ├── conftest.py                    \# Shared pytest fixtures**  
**│   ├── test\_auth.py                   \# Auth tests**  
**│   └── test\_item\_service.py           \# Item service tests**  
**│**  
**└── requirements.txt**

Explanation

* app/\_\_init\_\_.py  
  \_\_init\_\_.py should contain imports that keep the top level clean

* app/[main.py](http://main.py) (Used libraries: FastAPI)  
  [main.py](http://main.py) is the core of the application. It should contain middleware (e.g for logging), initialisation of the FastAPI application itself, initialisation and prepopulation of the database if needed, S3 instance, and **registration of the API Routers.**

* app/env  
  .env should contain all the **secrets and configuration for development. It should be git-ignored when pushed**  
    
* app/features/use\_case\_name/routers (Used libraries: FastAPI, Pydantic) | (Inject: Service)  
  The routers directory organises API endpoints by domain or feature. For instance, all inventory-related operations \- such as deleting, updating, or viewing inventory \- are grouped under  
  [inventory.py](http://inventory.py) using an APIRouter. These routers are then included in main.py. Their role is to serve as the **interface layer**: they handle reques**t validation, routing, and response formatting**, but **all business logic should be implemented in the service layer**.  
    
* app/features/use\_case\_name/models (Used libraries: SQLAlchemy)   
  This directory contains all the different database models (tables) as well as the actual database class. They consist of classes/objects that represent tables **through SQLAlchemy. Note that for clean architecture, they SHOULD NOT be directly interacted with in the routes and should only be used in repositories for data processing and retrieval.**  
    
* app/features/use\_case\_name/repositories (Used libraries: SQLAlchemy \- db queries) | (Inject: db session)  
  This directory defines repositories that act as the **source of truth for data**. They handle all direct interactions with the database, including creating, reading, updating, and deleting records. Business rules should not be implemented here.  
    
* app/features/use\_case\_name/services **(Used libraries: None)** | (Inject: adapters, repositories)  
  This directory defines services that implement the **core business logic** of the application. Services interact with repositories to read/write data and may call external APIs (such as S3 or Keycloak) as needed. They encapsulate rules and workflows, ensuring that routers remain thin and focused only on HTTP handling, while repositories remain focused on data persistence  
    
* app/infrastructure/adapters (Used libraries: Boto3, keycloak-python, other adapters if needed)  
  This directory contains infrastructure adapters that wrap external services such as Keycloak and S3 behind clean Python classes. Adapters are instantiated once in shared/dependencies.py and injected throughout the application via FastAPI's dependency injection system. Feature services and routers consume them through Depends() \- they interact with the adapter's interface without knowing anything about the underlying library (boto3, python-keycloak, etc.).  
    
* app/features/use\_case\_name/schemas (Used libraries: Pydantic)  
  The schemas directory contains **Pydantic models** used for request validation and response formatting. Schemas define the **data contract** between the API and its clients and **should not contain business logic or database operations**.  
    
* app/shared/utils (Used libraries: UUID, random, datetime etc.)  
  Utilities are convenient methods that are shared across your application, such as formatting date/time strings, UUID generators, random number generators, reading files, file path parsing, and mathematical functions. If possible, you should abstract them to other places of the application if it’s a necessity.  There is no need to use Dependency Injection for these methods.  
    
* app/shared/exceptions   
  Contains exceptions that can be raised or caught by multiple layers. Centralising exceptions here ensures consistent error handling across features, domain logic, and infrastructure, reduces duplication, and keeps feature and infrastructure layers decoupled. **This is the only file that technically breaks clean architecture as it leaks implementations (e.g allowing status codes in exception classes, however to reduce verbosity, this was a compromise.**  
    
* app/shared/[middleware.py](http://middleware.py) (Used libraries: FastAPI)  
  Middleware is reserved for concerns that genuinely need to run on every request regardless of route:  
* Request/response logging (timing, status codes, paths)  
* CORS headers (via FastAPI's built-in `CORSMiddleware`)  
* Request ID injection (attaching a trace/correlation ID for observability)  
  If your application needs none of these, this file may remain empty.  
  Authentication and authorisation must not be implemented as middleware. Use FastAPI's `Depends()` system instead \- it integrates with the DI framework, generates OpenAPI docs automatically, and applies selectively per route rather than running on every request.  
    
* apps/shared/[config.py](http://config.py) (Used libraries: Pydantic)  
  [Config.py](http://Config.py) declares all environment variables as a typed Pydantic Settings class. The only place in the application that reads from the environment and no other file should call os.environ directly.  
    
* app/shared/[dependencies.py](http://dependencies.py) | app//features/use\_case/dependencies (Used libraries: FastAPI \- Depends) **Important for DI**  
  This is the sole place where repositories, services, and adaptors are instantiated and wired together. Instantiation must not happen elsewhere \- not in routers, not in service classes, not inline in route handlers.  
  If a class requires credentials or configuration (keys, endpoints, secrets), it is constructed here using environment variables:

|    \# app/shared/dependencies.py   from fastapi import Depends   from adapters.s3\_adapter import S3Adapter   def get\_s3\_adapter() \-\> S3Adapter:       \# You can load config from .env       bucket\_name \= "my-bucket"       region \= "us-east-1"       return S3Adapter(bucket\_name=bucket\_name, region=region) |
| :---- |


* requirements.txt  
  This is very important for every Python developer to know. It allows the installation of all required dependencies of the application, all with one command. This saves a lot of time for the developer as it reduces the chances of runtime errors.

### **Handling Configuration In The Backend (Best Practices)** {#handling-configuration-in-the-backend-(best-practices)}

[***For secret/configuration naming conventions, please refer to Configruation & Secret Management Section***](#configuration-&-secret-key-management)

All environment variables are declared in a single `Settings` class using `pydantic-settings` in **app/shared/config.py**.The `settings` object is instantiated once at module level and imported wherever configuration is needed \- `os.environ` is never read directly anywhere else in the codebase.

| class Settings(BaseSettings):    DATABASE\_URL:           str       \= "sqlite:///./test.db"    KEYCLOAK\_REALM:         str    KEYCLOAK\_URL:           str    KEYCLOAK\_CLIENT\_SECRET: SecretStr \= SecretStr("")    S3\_ACCESS\_KEY:          SecretStr \= SecretStr("")    CORS\_ORIGINS:           list\[str\] \= \["http://localhost:5173"\]settings \= Settings() |
| :---- |

A few things worth noting about how this is structured. Fields without defaults \- such as `KEYCLOAK_REALM` and `KEYCLOAK_URL` \-  are required. **If they are absent from the environment, the application will refuse to start entirely rather than failing silently at runtime when those values are first accessed. This is intentional.**

Sensitive values such as client secrets and access keys use `SecretStr` rather than plain `str`. `SecretStr` masks the value in logs and string representations \- the `__str__` method on the `Settings` class demonstrates this, printing `**masked**` in place of any `SecretStr` field. This means you can safely log the full configuration at startup for debugging without leaking credentials.

### **Architecturing Your Classes And Components** {#architecturing-your-classes-and-components}

![][image22]

#### 

#### Introduction {#introduction}

This section will focus on the clean architecture needed to make collaboration easier. One rule of thumb is to write not for yourself but for the reader. This document will introduce how to implement the architecture components stated on top

#### Concrete Example (All the architecture components should be in their respective files) {#concrete-example-(all-the-architecture-components-should-be-in-their-respective-files)}

This is a simple example that will show how the components together fulfill a single usecase of the user uploading their profile picture. Hopefully, this example will help the author understand how all the components integrate.

##### **UI Layer** \- FastAPI Router {#ui-layer---fastapi-router}

| @router.post("", response\_model=ItemResponse, status\_code=201)def create\_item(    item\_data: ItemCreateRequest,    claims: TokenClaims \= Depends(get\_current\_user),    service: ItemService \= Depends(get\_item\_service),):    return service.create\_item(item\_data.title, item\_data.description, claims.sub) |
| :---- |

Only the router handles the request and response of the interface, and only the service is injected via `Depends()`. Pydantic is used for structured payload data \- `ItemCreateRequest` validates the incoming fields before the handler runs, giving clear validation and separation of concerns. The router only needs to know that it will fulfil the `create_item` role, with the internals abstracted away.

`TokenClaims` follows the same pattern. Rather than passing a raw token string or a user ID from the request, the router declares a `claims: TokenClaims = Depends(get_current_user)` dependency, which resolves the validated token into a typed object before the route handler runs. The router doesn't know or care how authentication works \- it simply receives a `TokenClaims` instance and extracts what it needs, typically `claims.sub`, which is the Keycloak user ID of the authenticated caller. This keeps authentication concerns out of the route body entirely, and means every route that declares this dependency is automatically protected \- if the token is missing or invalid, the dependency raises a `401` before the handler is ever reached.

This is more idiomatic than using a middleware 

##### **Domain Layer** \- Service {#domain-layer---service}

The service is the home of business logic. It receives plain values from the router, enforces rules, coordinates between the repository and any adapters, and returns a Pydantic model. It has no knowledge of FastAPI, HTTP, or how the data will be rendered.

| class ItemService:    def \_\_init\_\_(self, repository: ItemRepository, s3\_client=None):        self.repository \= repository        self.s3\_client \= s3\_client    def create\_item(self, title: str, description: str | None, keycloak\_user\_id: str) \-\> ItemResponse:        sanitised\_title \= title.strip()        sanitised\_description \= description.strip() if description else ""        if len(sanitised\_title) \== 0:            raise InvalidItemTitle("Title must have more than 0 characters")        if len(sanitised\_title) \> 30:            raise InvalidItemTitle("Title exceeds 30 characters")        if len(sanitised\_description) \> 100:            raise InvalidItemDescription("Description exceeds 100 characters")        item \= self.repository.create\_item(sanitised\_title, sanitised\_description, keycloak\_user\_id)        return self.\_resolve(item) |
| :---- |

Notice that no libraries are imported directly \- only the repository and the S3 adapter are injected. The service doesn't know how items are stored, or how files are uploaded. It only knows the rules: titles must be non-empty and under 30 characters, descriptions under 100\. Violations raise typed domain exceptions, not HTTP errors. It is the router's responsibility to catch those and map them to the appropriate status codes.

The same pattern applies to `upload_file` \- the service checks that uploads are configured, verifies the item exists and belongs to the caller, handles the old file cleanup, and delegates the actual upload to the adapter. The business rule lives here; the mechanism lives elsewhere.

| def \_resolve(self, item: Item) \-\> ItemResponse:    image\_url: str | None \= None    if item.image\_url and self.s3\_client:        image\_url \= self.s3\_client.generate\_presigned\_url(item.image\_url)    return ItemResponse(        id\=item.id,        title\=item.title,        description\=item.description,        owner\_id\=item.owner\_id,        image\_url\=image\_url,    ) |
| :---- |

Note: This is inside the service class 

**The `_resolve` method** is where the translation boundary discussed earlier is applied in practice. The repository returns a SQLAlchemy `Item` model \- a database object. The service cannot return that directly to the router, both because it exposes persistence internals and because the `image_url` stored in the database is a raw S3 object key, not something a client can use. `_resolve` converts the `Item` into an `ItemResponse` (Pydantic), and in doing so, runs the one piece of business logic that must happen on every read: exchanging the stored key for a fresh presigned URL.

![][image23]  
**Translation between Responsitory and Router. The router is then safe to return the ItemResponse which automatically returns it as an HTTP Response.** 

##### **Data Layer** \- Repository {#data-layer---repository}

| class ItemRepository:    def \_\_init\_\_(self, db: Session):        self.db \= db    def create\_item(self, title: str, description: str, keycloak\_user\_id: str) \-\> Item:        try:            item \= Item(title=title, description=description, owner\_id=keycloak\_user\_id)            self.db.add(item)            self.db.commit()            self.db.refresh(item)            return item        except SQLAlchemyError as e:            self.db.rollback()            raise DatabaseUnavailable("Failed to create item") from e |
| :---- |

The repository handles all interaction between the application and the database. It encapsulates infrastructure concerns \- managing transactions and commits, constructing queries, and ensuring entities exist before operating on them \- so the domain layer never has to think about any of this. The service calls `create_item` and receives a SQLAlchemy `Item` back; it has no knowledge of how that item was persisted, what the underlying query looked like, or how the session was managed.

You can also combine repositories if you require multiple tables to interact with one another, often in complex applications. For example, User \+ Inventory Repository \= UserInventory Repository if the use case is used a lot.

##### **Data Layer** \- Adapter {#data-layer---adapter}

| class KeycloakAdapter:    def \_\_init\_\_(        self,        server\_url: str \= settings.KEYCLOAK\_URL,        realm: str \= settings.KEYCLOAK\_REALM,        client\_id: str \= settings.KEYCLOAK\_CLIENT\_ID,        client\_secret: SecretStr \= settings.KEYCLOAK\_CLIENT\_SECRET,        cert\_filepath: str \= settings.KEYCLOAK\_CERT\_FILEPATH,    ):        self.server\_url \= server\_url        self.realm \= realm        self.client\_id \= client\_id        self.client\_secret \= client\_secret        self.cert\_filepath \= cert\_filepath        self.\_public\_key\_cache: str | None \= None        self.\_openid\_client: KeycloakOpenID | None \= None    def verify\_user\_token(self, user\_token: str) \-\> tuple\[bool, TokenClaims | None\]:        ... |
| :---- |

`get_current_user` is the dependency declared on every protected route. It extracts the `Authorization` header, passes it to the adapter for verification, and either returns a typed `TokenClaims` object or raises a `401` — before the route handler runs. The router never calls the adapter directly; it only ever sees the resolved `TokenClaims`.

`KeycloakAdapter` is instantiated in `dependencies.py` with all credentials sourced from settings. It caches the realm's public key in `_public_key_cache` so it isn't fetched from Keycloak on every request — only on first use or when a token signature mismatch suggests a key rotation has occurred.

| def get\_current\_user(    authorization: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials \= Depends(\_http\_bearer),    adapter: KeycloakAdapter \= Depends(get\_keycloak\_adapter),) \-\> TokenClaims:    valid, claims \= adapter.verify\_user\_token(authorization)    if not valid or claims is None:        raise HTTPException(status\_code=401, detail="Invalid or missing token")    return claims |
| :---- |

### **Dependency Injection** {#dependency-injection}

![][image24]  
*Dependency Injection Graph*

When using Clean Architecture, using a dependency injection library can help keep your code clean. If your service requires a lot of dependencies, it is more troublesome to manually instantiate your dependent classes. For example:

| \#Without DI Library for every instantiation     db \= SessionLocal()    repo \= UserRepository(db)    s3 \= S3Adapter()    keycloak \= KeycloakAdapter()    UserService(repo, s3, keycloak) |
| :---- |

It may not seem as troublesome as first, but keep in mind that you have to do it for testing or any isolation test. And when you want to add another dependency, you have to change your constructor and change every single instance of where the UserService is instantiated.

However, with FastAPI's “Depends” feature, dependency injection is made easier and you do not have to modify every single instance if you change the constructor of the service or repositories. For example:

| def get\_item\_service(    repository: ItemRepository \= Depends(get\_item\_repository),    s3: S3Adapter \= Depends(get\_s3\_adapter),) \-\> ItemService:    return ItemService(repository, s3) |
| :---- |

**The same pattern applies to authentication**. `get_current_user` declares a dependency on `get_keycloak_adapter`, verifies the token, and either returns a typed `TokenClaims` or raises a `401` — before the route handler runs:

| def get\_current\_user(    authorization: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials \= Depends(\_http\_bearer),    adapter: KeycloakAdapter \= Depends(get\_keycloak\_adapter),) \-\> TokenClaims:    valid, claims \= adapter.verify\_user\_token(authorization)    if not valid or claims is None:        raise HTTPException(status\_code=401, detail="Invalid or missing token")    return claims |
| :---- |

\*Note :`_http_bearer` will automatically extract the token from the `Authorization` header and validate that it is a Bearer scheme, returning an `HTTPAuthorizationCredentials` object. This means `get_current_user` never has to parse the header manually \- it receives the credentials directly and passes them straight to the adapter for verification.

Both are then declared on the route, and FastAPI resolves everything before `create_item` runs:

| @router.post("", response\_model=ItemResponse, status\_code=201)def create\_item(    item\_data: ItemCreateRequest,    claims: TokenClaims \= Depends(get\_current\_user),    service: ItemService \= Depends(get\_item\_service),):    return service.create\_item(item\_data.title, item\_data.description, claims.sub) |
| :---- |

If `ItemService` later requires a new dependency, only `dependencies.py` needs to change \- the router picks it up automatically. This is also why instantiation must not happen outside `dependencies.py`: the moment you construct a service inline elsewhere, you break the single point of change that makes this pattern valuable.

[Tutorial On FastAPI Depends (DI)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f270BoTicMA)

[Documentation on DI](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/)

### **Middleware**  {#middleware}

Middleware is reserved for concerns that genuinely need to run on every request and response regardless of route \- such as logging, CORS, and request ID injection. Authentication is intentionally not handled here; it belongs in `dependencies.py` via `Depends()`, as covered in the previous section.

A logging middleware is a good example of something that belongs here \- it wraps every request, measures its duration, and logs the outcome without any route needing to know about it:

| \# app/shared/middleware.pyimport timeimport loggingfrom fastapi import Requestlogger \= logging.getLogger(\_\_name\_\_)async def logging\_middleware(request: Request, call\_next):    start \= time.perf\_counter()    response \= await call\_next(request)    duration \= time.perf\_counter() \- start    logger.info(        "%s %s %s %.3fs",        request.method,        request.url.path,        response.status\_code,        duration,    )    return response |
| :---- |

And then attach it to FastAPI in [app.py](http://app.py)

| \# app/app.py@app.middleware("http")async def \_logging(request: Request, call\_next):    return await logging\_middleware(request, call\_next) |
| :---- |

Every request passes through this before reaching any route handler, and every response passes back through it on the way out \- making it the right place for cross-cutting concerns that have no business logic attached.

### **Naming Conventions** {#naming-conventions-1}

To bring structure, consistency, and clarity at a code level, you should follow the standard conventions. By doing so, it will reduce cognitive load and help the developer search for code more easily.

**Immutable Variables**  
Constants should be all capitalised (e.g TIMEOUT\_MAX\_SECONDS)

**Mutable Variables**  
Mutable variables should be lowercase snake case following PEP8 (E.g this\_is\_a\_variable)

**Functions**  
Functions should use lower case snake case (E.g this\_is\_a\_function)

**Classes**  
Classes should use pascal case following PEP8 (E.g ThisIsAClass)

**Exceptions**  
Exceptions should use pascal case (E.g AuthenticationError)

**File Names**  
File names should be in lower case snake case (E.g this\_is\_a\_file)

**Packages & Modules**  
Packages and modules should use lowercase snake case 

## Error Handling  {#error-handling}

Errors should be handled in different ways across the different layers. One can use exceptions.py to store custom errors such as Domain Errors.

| Layer | Responsibility for errors |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Data Layer (Repositories / Adapters)** | **Catch errors** related to persistence, external services, or invalid input from infra (DB, S3, Keycloak) and **raise meaningful exceptions that don’t leak implementation**. Don’t make business decisions. |
| **Domain / Service Layer** | Exceptions from adapters/repositories should generally be allowed to bubble up. Errors from below should not be caught and raised again to reduce boilerplate. Exceptions that need to be raised are domain-level errors (not enough funds etc) |
| **Presentation Layer (Routers / UI)** | Catch exceptions from the domain layer, format responses (HTTP status codes, messages), and handle user-facing errors. |

Custom errors must carry **clear semantic meaning** and be propagated from the repository layer through the service layer and then to the router, where they are handled and then sent to the frontend. Error naming should be driven by use cases and domain intent, **not by implementation details or internal application mechanics** (e.g DatabaseMissingRowsError, SQLAlchemyError) but instead **UserNotFoundError or UserPermissionsError**

As a guideline if you use an if statement that sets boundaries on the value itself (e.g 3 \< x \< 9 or xx \> \-1), that is business logic and raising that exception should be in the services (domain layer) instead of the data layer. 

### Designing Exceptions  {#designing-exceptions}

There are a few things to implement when designing the exceptions.

* There should be a base application exception class to blueprint exception data (Status codes, stack data, error message)  
* FastAPI handler to translate classes that inherits the base class into HTTP errors  
* The custom exceptions itself  
* Handle exceptions that are not caught but have the same interface as the app exceptions

Setting up the errors should be something like this:

### Exception class {#exception-class}

| \# app/shared/exceptions.pyclass ApplicationException(Exception):    """Base class for all custom app errors"""    def \_\_init\_\_(self, message: str, http\_status: int \= 500, details: dict | None \= None):        super().\_\_init\_\_(message)        self.message \= message        self.http\_status \= http\_status        self.details \= details or {}class UserNotFoundError(ApplicationException):    def \_\_init\_\_(self, user\_id: int):        message \= f"User with ID {user\_id} not found."        super().\_\_init\_\_(message, http\_status=404)class InsufficientFundsError(ApplicationException):    def \_\_init\_\_(self, message: str \= "Not enough money in account."):        super().\_\_init\_\_(message, http\_status=400)class DataStorageError(ApplicationException):    def \_\_init\_\_(self, message: str \= "Database is currently unreachable."):        super().\_\_init\_\_(message, http\_status=503) |
| :---- |

### FastAPI Exception Handler {#fastapi-exception-handler}

| \# app/main.pyfrom fastapi import FastAPI, Requestfrom fastapi.responses import JSONResponsefrom app.shared.exceptions import ApplicationExceptionapp \= FastAPI()\# Global handler for all Exceptions that contain the base class@app.exception\_handler(ApplicationException)async def global\_exception\_handler(request: Request, exc: ApplicationException):    return JSONResponse(        status\_code=exc.http\_status,        content={            "message": exc.message,            "details": exc.details,            "path": str(request.url)        }    )\# Global handler for unhandled exceptions@app.exception\_handler(Exception)async def global\_unhandled\_exception\_handler(request: Request, exc: Exception):    return JSONResponse(        status\_code=500,        content={            "message": "Internal Server Error",            "details": str(exc),            "path": str(request.url)        }    ) |
| :---- |

[You can read more here](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/#add-custom-headers)

#### When Do You Catch Exceptions？ {#when-do-you-catch-exceptions？}

In addition to handling errors at the router (UI) layer, implementation-specific exceptions (For example, SQLAlchemy failures surface as exceptions rather than return values, so they must be handled using exception handling rather than conditional checks.) should be caught earlier and translated into application-level exceptions to prevent infrastructure details from leaking upward. 

**In this design, repository exceptions are not caught in the service/domain layer especially if it’s raised with a custom exception in the application.** Catching them and raising another exception there would add unnecessary boilerplate, so **exceptions are allowed to bubble up to the API layer,** where they can be logged, transformed, or returned as standardised error responses **automatically using the fast API handler.** This reduces confusion compared to catching and raising exceptions on every layer and reduces human errors.

An example is shown for User Repository below:

| class UserRepository:    def \_\_init\_\_(self, db: Session):        self.db \= db    def get\_by\_id(self, user\_id: int):        try:            \# .one() raises NoResultFound if nothing is found (default err)            return self.db.query(User).filter(User.id \== user\_id).one()                except NoResultFound:            \# Translate technical NoResultFound into domain 'UserNotFoundError'            raise UserNotFoundError(f"User with ID {user\_id} does not exist.")                except SQLAlchemyError:            \# Prevent DB connection errors/impl from leaking upwards            raise DataStorageError("The database is currently unreachable.") |
| :---- |

| \# app/features/users/servicefrom app.shared.exceptions import UserNotFoundError, InsufficientFundsErrorclass UserService:    def \_\_init\_\_(self, user\_repo: UserRepository):        self.user\_repo \= user\_repo    def transfer\_money(self, user\_id: int, amount: float):        \# Can raise UserNotFoundError from the Repo        user \= self.user\_repo.get\_by\_id(user\_id)                 \# Logic-specific error (Not database error, it's a business logic constraint)        if user.balance \< amount:            raise InsufficientFundsError("Not enough money in account.") |
| :---- |

        

| from fastapi import APIRouter, Dependsfrom .services import UserServicerouter \= APIRouter()@router.post("/users/{user\_id}/transfer")def transfer(user\_id: int, amount: float, service: UserService \= Depends()):    \# No try/except required, the handler will handle it for you    return service.transfer\_money(user\_id, amount) |
| :---- |

As you can see this significantly reduces boilerplate as you do not have to catch and raise at every single layer. 

### Error Handling Behaviours {#error-handling-behaviours}

After we define custom error types, we need to know how to handle errors for production-ready code. In all languages, errors will cause the software to panic in case it is unhandled, and is not allowed in production unless the error is caused by the failure of a core dependency of the entire codebase. Error handling behaviour is generally a complex topic since it can vary between softwares. These examples are merely guidelines on how to handle common errors in your code \- not just frontend but also your applications.

This section will be heavily inspired by Rust’s Result type, which forces developers to decide whether to handle the error or perpetuate the error upstream. If designing libraries, you should also consider wrapping the error in a custom error type specific to your library, e.g.

| let connection \= CONNECTION\_POOL.get().unwrap\_or\_else(|err| {    return MyCustomError::new("error message")    }) |
| :---- |

## Frontend Clean Code Architecture {#frontend-clean-code-architecture}

### **Frontend Architecture Overview** {#frontend-architecture-overview}

![][image25]

The frontend, although all are categorised as the UI layer in the general application architecture, they also should be split between layers like the backend to maintain a sense of consistency. 

![][image26]

Inspired by: [https://github.com/alan2207/bulletproof-react/blob/master/docs/project-structure.md](https://github.com/alan2207/bulletproof-react/blob/master/docs/project-structure.md)

The layers in specific features should not be shared amongst other features. If you do need to share functionality with other features, it is best to put the functionaltiy into the shared file to let your team know that it might affect multiple dependencies. 

#### Grouping Features {#grouping-features}

**![][image27]**  
As mentioned, similar to the backend, frontend features should be split based on how much they affect one another. A feature represents a cohesive unit of user-facing functionality that can evolve largely independently of other features.

In the frontend, a single feature may span multiple pages, routes, services, hooks, and UI components. These elements are grouped together not because **they share a technical role or business logic in itself, but because they change together and serve the same user goal.**

To give one example of feature grouping, take authentication (login and register) for example. The **user’s goal is to gain access to the system.** As they use similar services and affect one another, login and register should be one feature (authentication).

Another example is viewing a user. You might want to view one user or you might want an overview. However the use case can be the same and two pages/routes can be in the same feature   
e.g

**└── pages/         \# Feature route-level components**  
       **└── UsersPage.jsx**  
       **├── ViewUserPage.js**

By defining feature boundaries this way, changes to one feature (for example, modifying user-related flows or API calls) are less likely to impact unrelated features such as inventory or reporting. This reduces coupling, improves maintainability, and makes the codebase easier to reason about as it grows.

### **Structuring the Frontend Files** {#structuring-the-frontend-files}

#### Frontend folder {#frontend-folder}

As the name suggests, the frontend folder should only contain frontend-related code, builds, and libraries. Within the frontend folder, there should be things such as:

**architecture-project-frontend/**  
**│**  
**├── src/**  
**│   │**  
**│   ├── assets/                          \# Static assets (images, icons, fonts)**  
**│   │   └── react.svg**  
**│   │**  
**│   ├── main.tsx                         \# Application entry point**  
**│   ├── index.css                        \# Global base styles**  
**│   ├── App.css                          \# App-level styles**  
**│   │**  
**│   ├── router/                          \# Route definitions**  
**│   │   └── index.tsx**  
**│   │**  
**│   ├── core/                            \# App infrastructure — bootstraps the entire application**  
**│   │   ├── api/                         \# Shared HTTP client**  
**│   │   │   └── client.ts**  
**│   │   ├── auth/                        \# Authentication setup (Keycloak)**  
**│   │   │   ├── AuthProvider.tsx**  
**│   │   │   └── keycloak.ts**  
**│   │   ├── components/                  \# App-level structural components**  
**│   │   │   ├── NavBar.tsx**  
**│   │   │   ├── ProtectedRoute.tsx**  
**│   │   │   └── AdminRoute.tsx**  
**│   │   ├── providers/                   \# Global React context providers**  
**│   │   │   └── AppProviders.tsx**  
**│   │   └── types/                       \# Shared TypeScript types and interfaces**  
**│   │       ├── api.ts**  
**│   │       └── auth.ts**  
**│   │**  
**│   ├── features/                        \# Feature-based modules**  
**│   │   ├── items/**  
**│   │   │   ├── components/              \# Feature-specific UI components**  
**│   │   │   │   └── ItemCard.tsx**  
**│   │   │   ├── hooks/                   \# Feature-specific hooks (TanStack Query)**  
**│   │   │   │   └── useItems.ts**  
**│   │   │   ├── services/                \# Client-side business logic**  
**│   │   │   │   ├── itemsService.ts**  
**│   │   │   │   └── itemsService.test.ts**  
**│   │   │   └── pages/                   \# Route-level components**  
**│   │   │       ├── DashboardPage.tsx**  
**│   │   │       └── ItemDetailPage.tsx**  
**│   │   │**  
**│   │   └── users/**  
**│   │       ├── hooks/**  
**│   │       │   └── ..**  
**│   │       ├── services/..**  
**│   │       │**     
**│   │       └── pages/..**  
**│   │**  
**│   └── shared/                          \# Reusable code shared across features**  
**│       ├── components/                  \# Custom generic UI components \+ shadcn/ui primitives**  
**│       │   ├── PageHeader.tsx**  
**│       │   └── ui/                      \# shadcn/ui primitives — managed by the shadcn CLI**  
**│       │       ├── button.tsx**  
**│       │       ├── card.tsx**  
**│       │       ├── dialog.tsx**  
**│       │       └── ...**  
**│       ├── hooks/                       \# Custom generic hooks \+ shadcn/ui hooks**  
**│       │   ├── useDebounce.ts**  
**│       │   └── use-mobile.ts            \# shadcn/ui — do not edit manually**  
**│       ├── lib/                         \# shadcn/ui utilities — do not edit manually**  
**│       │   └── utils.ts**  
**│       └── utils/                       \# Pure helper functions**  
**│           └── formatDate.ts**  
**│**  
**├── package.json**  
**├── package-lock.json**  
**└── .env**

#### Explanation {#explanation}

* src/core  
  Contains everything the application needs to start \- auth, the HTTP client, global providers, routing guards, and shared types. Nothing in core is feature-specific, and the rest of the application depends on it. Features and shared code must not be imported by core.

* src/core/api  
  Defines the shared Axios client used by all feature services. This is the single place where base URL configuration, authentication headers, and request/response interceptors are set up. Files here describe only *how* requests are made \- no business logic, response transformation, or UI behaviour belongs here.

* src/core/auth  
  Handles all authentication infrastructure. keycloak.ts initialises the Keycloak instance and exposes the client. AuthProvider.tsx wraps the application in a React context that makes the authenticated user and auth state available throughout the component tree. Nothing outside of core/auth should interact with Keycloak directly.

* src/core/components  
  App-level structural components that are not tied to any feature. NavBar.tsx renders the application navigation. ProtectedRoute.tsx and AdminRoute.tsx are routing guards that enforce authentication and role-based access \- they redirect unauthenticated or unauthorised users before the feature page renders.

* src/core/providers  
  AppProviders.tsx composes all global React context providers (auth, query client, theming, etc.) into a single wrapper mounted at the application root. Centralising providers here keeps main.tsx clean and makes the provider hierarchy easy to manage.

* src/core/types  
  Shared TypeScript types and interfaces used across the application. api.ts defines common API response shapes and error structures. auth.ts defines user and session types derived from Keycloak. Types here must not be feature-specific \- feature-level types live alongside their service files.  
  ---

* src/features/\<feature\>  
  Each feature is a self-contained module. A feature owns its pages, components, hooks, and services. Features may import from core, shared, and components/ui, but must not import from other features.

* src/features/\<feature\>/services  
  Implements client-side business logic for the feature. Services call core/api to make HTTP requests and are responsible for transforming, normalising, and filtering response data before it reaches the UI. This keeps pages and hooks focused on state and rendering, and keeps core/api focused purely on HTTP communication.

* src/features/\<feature\>/pages  
  Page-level components that correspond to application routes. Pages manage view-level state, delegate data fetching and mutations to hooks, and compose the feature's components into a complete screen. Pages must not call the API directly and should keep business logic minimal by delegating to services.

* src/features/\<feature\>/components  
  UI components scoped to the feature \- cards, forms, tables, and modals that are specific to this domain. Components should be presentational wherever possible, receiving data and callbacks via props. They must not perform API calls or contain business logic.

* src/features/\<feature\>/hooks *(optional)*  
  Custom hooks that sit between the service layer and the UI. They encapsulate data fetching, caching, mutation handling, error state, and loading state \- keeping pages and components focused on rendering. TanStack Query hooks belong here. This folder can be omitted for features with no meaningful state interactions.

  ---

* src/shared  
  Reusable code that is not tied to any feature and is not application infrastructure. The distinction from core is intent — core bootstraps the app, shared provides utilities that features consume. Anything in shared must be generic enough to be used by any feature without modification.

* src/shared/components  
  Custom reusable UI components built on top of components/ui primitives \- e.g. PageHeader, EmptyState, ConfirmDialog. These are not shadcn-generated; they are hand-crafted components that encode patterns used repeatedly across features. Components here must accept props that let each feature fill in its specific content, and must not contain any feature-specific logic.

* src/shared/hooks  
  Generic hooks reusable across any feature \- e.g. useDebounce, usePagination, useLocalStorage. Hooks here must not depend on any specific feature, API endpoint, or business domain. Feature-specific hooks live inside src/features/\<feature\>/hooks instead.

* src/shared/utils  
  Small, pure, stateless helper functions used across multiple features — formatting dates or numbers, validating inputs, parsing strings, generating IDs. Functions here have no dependency on any feature, component, or framework concept.  
  ---

* src/shared/components/ui *(shadcn/ui \- do not edit manually)*  
  Auto-generated shadcn/ui primitive components \- Button, Card, Dialog, Table, and so on. These are base-level building blocks that features and shared/components compose into higher-level UI. New primitives are added by running npx shadcn add \<component\> \- the output path is configured in components.json and will land here automatically. Do not hand-edit these files.

* src/shared/hooks/use-mobile.ts *(shadcn/ui \- do not edit manually)*  
  Auto-generated shadcn/ui hook. Managed by the shadcn CLI via the hooks alias in components.json.

* src/shared/lib *(shadcn/ui \- do not edit manually)*  
  Contains utils.ts, the shadcn/ui utility file that exposes the cn helper for merging Tailwind class names. Managed by the shadcn CLI via the lib alias in components.json.  
  ---

* src/router  
  Defines all application routes in one place. Maps URL paths to page-level components and applies routing guards from core/components. Keeping route definitions here rather than scattered across features makes the navigation structure of the app immediately visible.  
  ---

* src/assets  
  Static assets used throughout the application — images, icons, and fonts referenced directly in components or CSS.  
  ---

* src/index.css / src/App.css  
  Global styles and Tailwind base configuration. index.css defines CSS custom properties, base resets, and design tokens (colours, typography, spacing) that apply across the entire application. Consistent styling across pages should be driven from here, not from individual feature stylesheets.

**\*You don’t need pages if the feature is independent of that. For example notifications**

### **Feature-Based Routing Architecture** {#feature-based-routing-architecture}

![][image28]  
Routing for your pages (using react-router) should be based on your features/feature directory. For example if your pages are 

**│   ├── features/**            
**│   │   ├── users/**  
**│   │   │   └── pages/**           
**│   │   │       └── UsersList.jsx**  
**│   │   │       ├── ViewUserPage.jsx**

Routing should be users/xxx

|   { path: "/users", element: \<UsersList /\> },  { path: "/users/:id", element: \<ViewUser /\> }, |
| :---- |

This approach keeps related pages and logic together, making the structure **highly cohesive** and easier to maintain. It also makes routes more **predictable and discoverable**, as the folder structure mirrors the URL paths. Aligning feature directories with route paths reflects the **domain logic** of your application, so the URL structure naturally corresponds to the underlying data and functionality (e.g., `/users` for listing users, `/users/:id` for user details). This reduces accidental coupling between unrelated parts and supports **scalability**, allowing new features to be added with self-contained routes and components.

### **Authentication Architecture**  {#authentication-architecture}

[Relevant Sections for State Management & React Context](#passing-state)

#### Authentication Through Routes {#authentication-through-routes}

If the application requires authentication to access the app, it is highly recommended to implement authentication guards through routing. It is the most idiomatic and cleanest way to enforce authentication in your application.

![][image29]

#### 

#### Authentication Guards For Routing With Proxy Pattern {#authentication-guards-for-routing-with-proxy-pattern}

By wrapping `AppLayout` in with a custom **react component (shown as Protected Route)** at the top level, every child route inherits the authentication guard automatically \- there is no need to apply it per route. If a user is unauthenticated, `ProtectedRoute` redirects them to Keycloak before `AppLayout` or any of its children ever render. The coupled `/users` and `/items` prefixes also make it immediately clear which routes belong to which feature.

**export** **const** router \= createBrowserRouter(\[  
  {  
    element: \<**ProtectedRoute**\>\<**AppLayout** /\>\</**ProtectedRoute**\>,  
    children: \[  
      { path: '/', element: \<**DashboardPage** /\> },

**Internal Architecture And Mechanism Of ProtectedRoute Through Auth Context (Service Locator)**

`ProtectedRoute` works by wrapping an `AuthProvider`  **(which should be built to be accessed from all pages) \- a React Context that initialises Keycloak on mount and manages all auth state in one place.** Because it sits at the top of the tree, any component in the application can call `useAuth()` to read state such as whether the user is logged in, their user info, or whether they have an admin role \- without ever talking to Keycloak directly.

`ProtectedRoute` consumes that context and acts as the gatekeeper. Before any page renders, it resolves into one of three states:

* **Loading**:  Keycloak is still initialising, a spinner is shown.  
* **Access denied**:  the user is authenticated but not in the required group, an error screen is shown with a sign out option.  
* **Authorised**: the user passes all checks and the requested page renders.

![][image30]

#### **Accessing Auth Information Through AuthProvider (Context)** {#accessing-auth-information-through-authprovider-(context)}

As mentioned before in the previous section, AuthProvider should allow access to authentication information across the entire react tree such as IsAdmin, isAuthenticated. For example the potential usable values are:

|   const value: AuthContextValue \= {    isAuthenticated,    isAuthorized,    isAdmin,    isLoading,    userInfo: userInfo as Record\<string, unknown\> | null,    token: keycloak.token,    login: () \=\> keycloak.login(),    logout: () \=\> keycloak.logout(),  } |
| :---- |

One should then be able to access the values in any pages without hoisting any data through React Contexts, such as 

| export default function AdminRoute({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {  const { isAdmin } \= useAuth()  if (\!isAdmin) {    return (      \<div className="flex flex-col items-center justify-center h-screen gap-2"\>        \<h1 className="text-2xl font-semibold"\>Access Denied\</h1\>        \<p className="text-muted-foreground"\>You need admin permissions to view this page.\</p\>      \</div\>    )  } |
| :---- |

### **Using Types And Interfaces For Type-Safety** {#using-types-and-interfaces-for-type-safety}

TypeScript types and interfaces give shape to the data flowing through the application \- API responses, component props, and auth state all benefit from being explicitly typed rather than inferred as `any`.

Shared types that are used across the application live in `core/types/`:

|  export interface AuthContextValue {   isAuthenticated: boolean   isAuthorized: boolean   isAdmin: boolean   userInfo: Record\<string, unknown\> | null   token: string | undefined   login: () \=\> void   logout: () \=\> void } |
| :---- |

Feature-specific types \- such as the shape of an item returned from the API \- live alongside the feature they belong to:

| // features/items/services/itemsService.ts export interface ItemResponse {   id: number   title: string   description: string   owner\_id: string   image\_url: string | null }  |
| :---- |

The practical benefit is that when the backend changes a response shape, TypeScript surfaces every affected call site immediately rather than letting the mismatch silently reach the UI. Types also make hooks and components self-documenting \- a function signature that returns `ItemResponse[]` tells the next developer exactly what to expect without reading the implementation.

### **Architecturing Your Classes And Components** {#architecturing-your-classes-and-components-1}

**![][image31]**

#### Introduction {#introduction-1}

This part will show in detail how various parts of the app are architected and what functions you should put in specific architecture components in order to maintain separation of concerns. 

#### Concrete Example (All the architecture components should be in their respective files) {#concrete-example-(all-the-architecture-components-should-be-in-their-respective-files)-1}

This is a simple example that will show how the components together fulfill a single usecase. Hopefully, this example will help the author understand how all the components integrate. Do refer to the image on top, as it follows the layers of API interface \-\> Service \-\> Custom Hooks \-\> Pages \- \- \-\> components  
                                                                                        

**API Layer: In core/api/[client.js](http://client.js)** 

| apiClient.interceptors.request.use((config) \=\> {   if (keycloak.token) {     config.headers.Authorization \= \`Bearer ${keycloak.token}\`   }   return config }) apiClient.interceptors.response.use(   (response) \=\> response,   (error: AxiosError) \=\> {     if (error.code \=== 'ECONNABORTED') {       return Promise.reject(new Error('Request timed out — please try again'))     }     if (error.response?.status \=== 401) {       keycloak.login()     }     return Promise.reject(error)   } ) |
| :---- |

The client is the sole communicator from the frontend to the backend and all requests should go through the client. The client handles sending the token to the backend in the header as part of the authentication process (among other processes) through the usage of interceptors. In this example it also uses **keycloak-js** to retrieve the token from keycloak.

The API layer should not directly be used in pages but should be used in services where the business logic and transformation of data is handled.

**Service Layer: In features/\<your\_feature\>/services/[itemsService.ts](http://itemsService.ts)**

| export async function uploadItemFile(itemId: string | number, file: File): Promise\<{ url: string }\> {   const form \= new FormData()   form.append('file', file)   const { data } \= await apiClient.post\<{ url: string }\>(\`/items/${itemId}/upload\`, form, {     headers: { 'Content-Type': 'multipart/form-data' },   })   return data } |
| :---- |

The service layer is responsible for all communication with the backend \- constructing requests, setting the correct headers, and mapping the response into a shape the rest of the app can use. It has no knowledge of React, state, or the UI. In this case, `uploadItemFile` wraps the file in a `FormData` object (required for multipart uploads), calls the correct endpoint, and returns the URL. The `apiClient` handles attaching the Bearer token automatically, so the service only needs to express *what* it is sending, not *how* authentication works.

**Hook Layer: features/\<your\_feature\>/hooks/useUploadItemFile.tsx**

| export function useUploadItemFile(itemId: string | undefined) {   const queryClient \= useQueryClient()   return useMutation({     mutationFn: (file: File) \=\> uploadItemFile(itemId\!, file),     onSuccess: () \=\> queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: \['items'\] }),   }) } |
| :---- |

The hook layer is the bridge between the service (the data) and the page. It wraps service calls in TanStack Query \- either `useQuery` for reads or `useMutation` for writes \- and exposes the result as React state. The page calls the hook and gets back data, loading state, and error state without knowing anything about how the request was made or how the cache is managed. That detail stays in the hook.

**Component Layer (No functions):**  **features/\<your\_feature\>/components/ImageImageUpload.tsx**

| export function ItemImageUpload({ isPending, hasImage, onChange }: ItemImageUploadProps) {   return (     \<label className\={\`... ${isPending ? 'opacity-50 pointer-events-none' : 'hover:border-primary'}\`}\>       {isPending ? (         \<span\>Uploading…\</span\>       ) : (         \<\>           \<span\>{hasImage ? 'Replace image' : 'Upload image'}\</span\>         \</\>       )}       \<input type\="file" accept\="image/\*" onChange\={onChange} className\="hidden" /\>     \</label\>   ) }  |
| :---- |

The component layer should be purely presentational and should be stateless. THey receive props and render the UI. This component has no knoweldge of TanStack Query, the service, or the API. It only knows the states in itself. This is what keeps components reusable. 

**Page Level**: **features/\<your\_feature\>/pages/itemDetail.tsx**

| export default function ItemDetailPage() {   const { id } \= useParams\<{ id: string }\>()   const { data: item, isLoading, isError } \= useItem(id)   const upload \= useUploadItemFile(id)    function handleUpload(e: React.ChangeEvent\<HTMLInputElement\>) {     const file \= e.target.files?.\[0\]     if (\!file) return     upload.mutate(file, {       onSuccess: () \=\> toast.success('Image uploaded successfully'),       onError: (err) \=\> toast.error('Upload failed', { description: err.message }),     })   }    if (isLoading) return \<LoadingSpinner /\>   if (isError || \!item) return \<ErrorAlert message\="Item not found" /\>    return (     \<div className\="container mx-auto max-w-2xl py-8 px-4"\>       \<Card\>         \<CardContent\>           \<h1\>{item.title}\</h1\>           \<p\>{item.description}\</p\>           {item.image\_url && \<img src\={item.image\_url} alt\={item.title} /\>}           \<ItemImageUpload             isPending\={upload.isPending}             hasImage\={\!\!item.image\_url}             onChange\={handleUpload}           /\>         \</CardContent\>       \</Card\>     \</div\>   ) } |
| :---- |

The page should both use the component as well as the hooks and functions. The page passes down the state and relevant functions to the ItemImageUpload component.

### **Passing State** {#passing-state}

![][image32]In React, state is owned by the closest common ancestor that needs to manage or modify it. When components are nested, state is passed down as props to children that need to read it, and callback functions are passed down if children need to modify it. This keeps the ancestor as the single source of truth and keeps the components reusable if the application requires additional usages. 

**When components are 3–4 levels deep, passing props through every intermediate level becomes unwieldy.** In that case, **React Context provides a global state that any component in the tree can read** , without threading props through every level.

A practical example of this is authentication. `AuthProvider` wraps the entire application at the top of the tree and exposes auth state \- whether the user is logged in, their user info, their roles \- through context. Any component, regardless of how deeply nested, can call `useAuth()` to read that state without the parent needing to pass it down manually. This is also why `ProtectedRoute` works cleanly \- it simply calls `useAuth()` and acts on the result, with no props required.

See: [https://react.dev/learn/sharing-state-between-components](https://react.dev/learn/sharing-state-between-components)

### **Naming Conventions** {#naming-conventions-2}

To bring structure, consistency, and clarity at a code level, you should follow the standard conventions. By doing so, it will reduce cognitive load and help the developer search for code more easily.

**Immutable Variables**  
Constants should be all capitalised (e.g TIMEOUT\_MAX\_SECONDS)

**Mutable Variables**  
Mutable variables should be camel case (E.g thisIsAVariable)

**Functions**  
Functions should be camel case (E.g thisIsAFunction)

**Classes**  
Classes should use pascal case (E.g ThisIsAClass)

**Exceptions**  
Exceptions should use pascal case (E.g AuthenticationError)

**File Names**  
File names should be according to whether it’s a function or a class/component (depdent on the main entity).  
If it’s a component it should be in pascal case (E.g ThisIsAReactComponent)  
If it’s a function it should be in camel case (E.g thisIsAFunction)

### **Middleware** {#middleware-1}

Similar to the backend, you should use middleware for functions that need to be used for every request/response (e.g **authentication/logging).**

To use middleware you can register it in your **shared client**

| export const apiClient \= axios.create({  baseURL: "/api",  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },});// Middleware: add auth token to every requestapiClient.interceptors.request.use(  (config) \=\> {    const token \= localStorage.getItem("authToken"); // example: get token from storage    if (token) {      config.headers.Authorization \= \`Bearer ${token}\`;    }    return config;  },  (error) \=\> {    return Promise.reject(error);  }); |
| :---- |

Then import the client into your service 

### **Handling Errors** {#handling-errors}

Handling errors in the frontend is quite simple. You do not need to catch any exceptions or raise Error handling in the frontend is handled at the page level rather than propagating through every layer. The service and hook layers do not need try/catch blocks \- if a request fails, TanStack Query catches the error automatically and exposes it through `isError` and `error` on the hook's return value.

const { data, isLoading, isError, error } \= useUsers()

if (isError) return \<div\>{error.message}\</div\>

For mutations, errors are handled inline at the call site via `onError`:

| createItem.mutate(form, {   onSuccess: () \=\> {     setOpened(false)     setForm({ title: '', description: '' })     toast.success('Item created')   },   onError: (err) \=\> toast.error('Error', { description: err.message }), })  |
| :---- |

# 5\. Logging {#5.-logging}

### Why logs? {#why-logs?}

Logging is an important process in development. It helps developers reduce bugs and find unknown bugs that are not normally spotted. In a production environment, it is especially helpful as **production does not have Inspect Element in the browser for security reasons.** 

### ![][image33]

As shown on top of the document, it is recommended that you use the Python logging module for the backend and react-toastify or other notification libraries (because we cannot use console.log). In the future, this may change to more advanced methods of logging, such as remote logging (Sentry). As of now, the production environment does not have that kind of support.

*\*Based on the author’s experience you will have a tough time without logs*

### What To Log \- Backend {#what-to-log---backend}

You should log:

* Every HTTP Request Status, Data, User Agents etc  
* Every HTTP Response and Data and Stack Trace (For Exceptions)  
* Keys & Configuration Variables and whether they are all inside  
* Dangerous or persistent operations such as database prepopulations  
* Response times  
* Security Related Exceptions (Invalid tokens, forbidden access)  
* Handled exceptions and reason

### 

### What To Log \- Frontend {#what-to-log---frontend}

You should log:

* Configuration variables  
* Every HTTP Request Status, Data sent  
* Every HTTP Request Status, Data received  
* **Runtime Errors in UI & API errors caught**  
* Mutations in TanStack Query  
* Security Related Exceptions (Invalid tokens, forbidden access)

### How To Log {#how-to-log}

Apart from using the respective libraries stated in this document, **you should use middleware** (Already stated in this document above), to log every single request and response. **For example in axios (frontend), you should add a middleware to the axios client that logs request and responses. In the backend you should add a logging middleware to FastAPI.**

**Request Middleware in Axios (Runs every request)**

| client.interceptors.request.use((config) \=\> {  console.log(\`\[API Request\] ${config.method.toUpperCase()} ${config.url}\`, config.data || "");  return config;}, (error) \=\> {  console.error("\[API Request Error\]", error);  return Promise.reject(error);}); |
| :---- |

**Request MIddleware in FastAPI (Runs every request)**

| from fastapi import FastAPIfrom app.middleware.logging\_middleware import logging\_middlewareapp \= FastAPI()@app.middleware("http")async def request\_logging\_middleware(request: Request, call\_next):    start \= time.perf\_counter()    response \= await call\_next(request)    duration\_ms \= (time.perf\_counter() \- start) \* 1000    logger.info(        "%s %s \-\> %d (%.1fms)",        request.method,        request.url.path,        response.status\_code,        duration\_ms,    )    return response |
| :---- |

### Future/Potential Extensions Using Logger {#future/potential-extensions-using-logger}

Logger allows easy integration with other ways of logging such as generating .txt logs for analysis etc.

### Logging Caveats in Production {#logging-caveats-in-production}

* When logging to standard output there should be an option that should be added for ‘debug’. Check this if you cannot log to standard output.  
* There is no way to check console.log in production so the developer needs another method of logging.
