# 6\. Enforcing Code Quality & Application Quality {#6.-enforcing-code-quality-&-application-quality}

## Overview {#overview-2}

![][image34]  
Apart from setting standards and establishing knowledge management, ensuring that these practices are enforced requires some measures to be implemented. This section will go through the various ways and points at which code quality should be controlled at different stages of the development lifecycle. 

This document will first define the different points at which quality should be enforced:

* Onboarding Stage  
* Development Stage  
* Pull Request Stage  
* Continuous Integration Stage

## Onboarding Stage {#onboarding-stage}

### Overview {#overview-3}

This stage only happens once. When a new person comes into the SWE team they should familarise themselves with the standards we have such as the tech stack, development process and coding practices.

Before they come into the team they should

* Have some basic coding knowledge  
* Read this document (Tech stack, folder structure, design patterns, branch enforcement) & Be able to have a general understanding of it  
* Setup local development environment (text editor, linters, code formatters \- will be explained in development stage)  
* Walkthrough of template code/create demo code to synthesise all the knowledge here

Based on these requirements, new team members during their training phase should do majority of these things and get used to the process.

## Development Stage {#development-stage}

### Overview {#overview-4}

This stage essentially resides in your local machine and your editor. Before you even commit & push your local tools should be able to tell you any poor-quality code, poorly formatted code, and code smells. In order to do that, developers should enable and use tools that they have setup from the onboarding stage.

These tools include:

* Code formatters (prettier)  
* Linters (ESLint)  
* Static analysis tools  
* Basic testing/unit testing of new functionality

This is to reduce the chance of getting the merge/pull request rejected by the automated CI review and the senior developer. 

### Enforcing Linters & Formatters In Development Stage {#enforcing-linters-&-formatters-in-development-stage}

![][image35]

#### VSCode Workspace Recommendations {#vscode-workspace-recommendations}

VSCode Workspace Recommendations (.vscode/extensions.json) is a project-level file committed to the repository that contains a list of recommended extensions for the project. When a developer opens the project in VSCode for the first time, VSCode detects this file and displays a prompt asking them to install the recommended extensions. This ensures all developers have the correct extensions installed without having to manually search for them, keeping the team's editor setup consistent

#### VSCode extensions {#vscode-extensions}

Extensions are plugins installed into each developer's local VSCode. They act as the bridge between the editor and the underlying package \- without the extension installed, VSCode has no way to surface linting errors or trigger formatting. The extension itself does not define any rules or perform the actual checks; it simply connects the editor to the package and displays its output inline. This is why `extensions.json` exists \- to ensure every developer has the required extensions installed so that `settings.json` and the tool config files can actually take effect.

#### VSCode Workspace Settings  {#vscode-workspace-settings}

VSCode Workspace Settings (`.vscode/settings.json`) are project-level configuration files committed to the repository that control how the editor behaves for everyone working on the project. They do not add any new functionality \- instead they configure the extensions already installed, such as enabling ESLint, setting Prettier as the default formatter for JavaScript and TypeScript files, and setting Black as the default formatter for Python files. They also control editor behaviours triggered by those tools, such as automatically fixing ESLint errors and running the formatter on save. Because they are committed to the repo, all developers automatically get the same editor behaviour without having to configure their VSCode manually.

#### Tool Config Files (Also for CI/CD) {#tool-config-files-(also-for-ci/cd)}

Tool config files such as `.flake8`, `.prettierrc`, `pyproject.toml`, and `eslint.config.js` are separate from VSCode settings. **They define the actual rules and standards that the tools enforc**e, such as maximum line length, quote style, or which patterns to flag. These are read directly by the package itself \-  not by VSCode \- meaning they apply consistently whether the tool is run in the editor, the terminal, or the CI/CD pipeline.

#### 

## Merge/Pull Request Stage {#merge/pull-request-stage}

This stage is the most important stage out of all the stages as it involves a lead developer that makes sure all the code is up to standard as a formal review not just in terms of formatting but in terms of the architecture as a whole. The senior developer should refer to this document as the standard. This stage ensures that code quality, architectural integrity, security, and maintainability are preserved.

In order to enforce this there must be two types of reviews in this stage. 

### Overview {#overview-5}

To enforce this type of review, there should be a .github/workflows/ci.yml in Github (Github Actions). Github will then automatically run this on every PR and block the merge depending on the code/function. This reduces the burden on senior developers by automating routine validation tasks, allowing them to focus on higher-level architectural and business logic concerns during code review.

It should check for:

* Build verifications (Make sure the app compiles)  
* Linting (Code quality consistency)  
* Static code analysis (ES Lint, Flake8)  
* Dependency & Container vulnerabilities (Trivy)  
* Secret Scanning (Check for API Keys)  
* Unit tests for individual containers (No regressions) \- optional (?)

It should fix (if possible) for:

* Formatting issues (Automatically correct code formatting violations using Prettier etc)  
* Trivial code style/naming corrections (Fix simple style inconsistencies using static analysis)  
* Security & Dependency updates (Automatically upgrade dependencies to newer non-breaking versions to reduce vulnerabilities and apply minor security patches)

This reduces unnecessary merge rejections for resolvable issues and allows developers/reviewers to focus on high level design. 

### Enforcing Linters & Formatters In Request Stage {#enforcing-linters-&-formatters-in-request-stage}

You should enforce linters and formatters by using Github Workflows in development stage. This also works in line with the tool config files (follows linter rules) as mentioned in the development stage 

For example in .github/workflows: 

name: Lint & Format Check

on:  
  push:  
    branches: \[main\]  
  pull\_request:  
    branches: \[main\]

jobs:  
  frontend:  
    name: Frontend (ESLint \+ Prettier)  
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest  
    defaults:  
      run:  
        working-directory: architecture-project-frontend

    steps:  
      \- uses: actions/checkout@v4

      \- uses: actions/setup-node@v4  
        with:  
          node-version: 20  
          cache: npm  
          cache-dependency-path: architecture-project-frontend/package-lock.json

      \- name: Install dependencies  
        run: npm ci

      \- name: ESLint  
        run: npm run lint

      \- name: Prettier  
        run: npx prettier \--check .

Using GitHub workflows ensures that linting and formatting checks are enforced automatically on every push and pull request, without relying on individual developers to remember to run them locally. When a check fails, GitHub notifies the developer directly \- the pull request is marked as failing and the specific job output shows exactly which files and lines failed, making it straightforward to identify and fix the issue.

Beyond just catching problems, workflows can also be configured to automatically apply fixes where possible \- for example, running Prettier to reformat files and committing the result back to the branch. This reduces unnecessary back-and-forth where a merge is rejected purely for formatting reasons that could be resolved without human intervention.

### Senior Developer Reviewer {#senior-developer-reviewer}

The senior developer may check for linting etc. However, they should focus more on the higher level architecture and business logic concerns. Those functions cannot be simply scanned or checked by any tools. 

* **Protected branches** for the project (At least one senior developer must review the PR and the author of the PR cannot approve their own changes)  
* The reviewer must verify code follows **naming conventions, architectural standards and no unreadable/garbage code, sensitive data is exposed.**  
* If deemed not up to standard the senior developer should **reject the merge request.** 

## Continuous Deployment Stage (Pre-staging) {#continuous-deployment-stage-(pre-staging)}

As building all the containers using helm charts etc is slow and takes a long time, mock deploying the application from scratch in Github Actions is not recommended. 

Upon completing one phase of the application or when the team is sure that the architecture is solidified, a developer who is familiar with devops (OpenShift etc) should start building the helm charts and RFOs and start preparing the material.

Once the helm charts are done, the developer should be able to trial deploy it onto OpenShift.

WIP (We need a centralised server)

# 7\. Scalability {#7.-scalability}

Most of the time, your backend will never be exposed or accessible to the frontend. In these cases, you will use a reverse proxy such as [Caddy](https://caddyserver.com/), [Traefik](https://traefik.io/traefik) and [Nginx](https://nginx.org/). Most of the time, these services have more than 1 role. For example,

| Features | Caddy | Traefik | Nginx |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| TLS | Self Serves | Self Serves via Let’s Encrypt | Does not serve SSL. |
| Ease of config | Easy to setup from documentation | Easy to setup for docker but not baremetal | Hardest to configure |
| Ease of integration | Easy integration baremetal | Easy and well documented installation into k8s | Manual configuration required |
| Documentation | Documentation for Caddyfile (baremetal) | Documentation mostly for docker | Manual configuration for both |
| Performance | Little bit of overhead | Most overhead | Fastest |
| Other functions | File Sharing; | Rate Limiting | File Sharing; Rate Limiting; Proxy Caching |

## Load Balancer {#load-balancer}

Load balancers use different algorithms to distribute network traffic to different instances of the server. In certain cases, this will require a change of code structure, such as accessing a centralized database, or accessing data.

## Reverse Proxy {#reverse-proxy}

A reverse proxy is a proxy connection that receives the connection from your user, so they do not directly connect to the backend. This provides an additional level of security as you are able to block unwanted network traffic before sending the data to your backend.

# 8\. Testing {#8.-testing}

## Unit Testing {#unit-testing}

Unit Testing ties into clean architecture. The cleaner the architecture, the easier it is to test and isolate functionality to ensure that it works. Refer to the Clean Architecture section on how to make your code clean. 

## Penetration/Security Testing {#penetration/security-testing}

Penetration Testing needed to find loopholes in the software, and is usually done by a dedicated group with no prior knowledge of the software architecture. All developers should always keep security considerations and vulnerabilities in mind, and it should be reflected in the code. Here are the most common security vulnerabilities in 2025: [OWASP Top 10 2025](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/).

## Load Testing {#load-testing}

During development of your application, the scaling of the system must also be taken into consideration. Services such as [Redis](https://redis.io/) can greatly improve user data access speeds, but the database must fit into memory. Redis can also implement sharding, but it must be supported by your application. It can also behave as a reverse proxy.

# 9\. Security {#9.-security}

## Application Authentication {#application-authentication}

All backend endpoints enforce strict authentication and authorisation using Keycloak-issued tokens. Every API request must include a valid access token in the **Authorisation header**, which the backend decrypts and verifies before processing the request. This ensures that only authenticated users can access protected resources.

The backend checks:

* **Token validity** \- ensuring it was issued by Keycloak and has not expired  
* **User roles and permissions** \-  confirming the requester is authorized for the specific endpoint.

Requests with invalid, expired, or unauthorized tokens are rejected with **HTTP 401 Unauthorised** or **HTTP 403 Forbidden** responses.

**Best Practices:**

* Tokens are verified on every request to prevent unauthorised access.  
* Role-based access control is enforced consistently across endpoints.  
* Token expiration and refresh mechanisms reduce security risks while maintaining usability.  
* All communication occurs over HTTPS to protect tokens in transit.

This will ensure that no unauthorised users can access the frontend nor the backend.

Refer to related parts:  
[Keycloak Authentication Flow](#keycloak-token-based-auth-architecture-flow/stack)  
[Middleware](#middleware-1)

## Configuration & Secret Key Management {#configuration-&-secret-key-management}

### Environment/Secret Variables Naming Convention & Labelling {#environment/secret-variables-naming-convention-&-labelling}

Environment and secret variables should follow the standard practice of prefixing by responsibility. It is highly recommended that variables and th**eir naming conventions should not deviate across projects** to ensure that developers can work on each other's projects seamlessly with less friction. Standard credentials, including database passwords, authentication keys, and S3 secrets, **should remain consistent and not be changed,** not just the prefix itself.

\*Note that for

**Prefix by responsibility**

| Type | Prefix |
| ----- | ----- |
| App | `APP_` |
| DB | `DB_` |
| Auth | `KC_` |
| S3 | `S3_` |
| Infra | `INFRA_` |

**Mandatory Variables**

| `APP_ENV=prod APP_LOG_LEVEL=INFO APP_API_URL= DB_HOST= DB_PORT= DB_NAME= DB_USER= DB_PASSWORD= KC_ENDPOINT= KC_REALM= KC_CLIENT_ID= KC_CLIENT_SECRET= S3_ENDPOINT= S3_BUCKET= S3_ACCESS_KEY= S3_SECRET_KEY=` |
| :---- |

**`*Note for the frontend you need VITE in front of the env variable e.g`**  
**`VITE_KC_REALM for development environments when you’re using .env in the frontend`**

**Labelling Secrets and Configuration in Development**

As your secrets and configuration will both be in .env, your .env should also be organised in a way such that you can tell what counts as a config and what counts as a secret. 

For example 

**\# config**

| DB\_HOST=localhostDB\_PORT=5432DB\_NAME=app\_db |
| :---- |

**\# secrets**

| DB\_USER=app\_userDB\_PASSWORD=secretS3\_SECRET\_KEY=... |
| :---- |

That way, it will allow you to properly segment the secrets and configuration credentials when you go to staging and production, and not accidentally put secrets into config and vice versa. 

**You should also not put any secrets in the frontend so this only applies to the backend.**

### 

### Storing Your Secrets \- Development {#storing-your-secrets---development}

| Secrets (Backend only) | Configuration (Backend & Frontend) |
| :---- | :---- |
| .env  | .env  |

You should store your secrets and configuration in the environment file. Your file should be named **.env, and it should be git-ignored to prevent leakage of keys.** As your secrets and configuration will both be in .env, your .env should also be organised in a way such that you can tell what counts as a config and what counts as a secret. 

**Note that .env files should be stored separately in the frontend and backend in development. There should only be secrets in the backend and never the frontend because it can be exposed. Only keep configuration variables in the frontend.** 

### 

### Storing Your Secrets \- Production Ready {#storing-your-secrets---production-ready}

| Secrets (Backend only) | Configuration (Backend & Frontend) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Inject using open shift (secrets.yaml) | values.yaml |

When you use OpenShift, the process is slightly different. Do note that you also have to **.gitignore your .yaml files** when you are trying to use OpenShift, when trying to make your application ready for deployment.

You would then use secrets.yaml/values.yaml in deployment.yaml so that the values can be injected. You would have to do this separately for the frontend and backend. This means that the backend should have its own values/secrets.yaml, and the frontend should have its own values.yaml.

## Unwanted Privilege Escalation {#unwanted-privilege-escalation}

Unwanted privilege escalation refers to a user getting more access than they are supposed to. This can come in the form of horizontal escalation (getting access to other users) or vertical escalation (getting admin access). 

### Proper handling of user access and user access tokens {#proper-handling-of-user-access-and-user-access-tokens}

This can even come in the form of not properly logging a user out by keeping access tokens in browser cache or not redirecting them to the login page when accessing pages outside their permission.

An example of not redirecting the users back to the login page:

| export const logout \= () \=\> keycloak?.logout();const logout\_b \= async () \=\> {     await toast.promise(     new Promise(() \=\> {       logout();     }),     {       loading: "Logging you out...",       success: "Successfully logged out\!",       error: "Failed to logout",     }   ); }; |
| :---- |

### Keeping admin endpoints open or unsecured {#keeping-admin-endpoints-open-or-unsecured}

Security by obscurity is not enough to hide admin endpoints. Software such as [Gobuster](https://www.kali.org/tools/gobuster/) can easily break these endpoints. 

For commercial scale software, do not include your admin endpoints in [robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro). (See [wikipedia.org/robots.txt](http://wikipedia.org/robots.txt) as an example)

## Outdated or improper encryption methods {#outdated-or-improper-encryption-methods}

Most symmetric encryption methods are considered secure because it takes a lot of computation to crack such that it is unfeasible to crack in a reasonable amount of time. 

Outdated encryption methods usually exhibit a vulnerability such as collision attacks for SHA1 or bit flip attacks for AES CBC, just to name a few. **Research on vulnerabilities of encryption algorithms before using it.**

#### SHA1 {#sha1}

SHA1 was initially used for ensuring data integrity transmitted over the internet, using its digital fingerprint. However, it has been considered insecure due to collision attacks and [chosen-prefix collision attacks](https://crypto.stackexchange.com/questions/76941/how-a-chosen-prefix-collision-is-more-useful-than-a-standard-collision-concernin).   
Example of SHA1 collision attack: [sha-mbles.github.io/](http://sha-mbles.github.io/).

### AES-CBC {#aes-cbc}

For similar reasons, modern day encryption methods no longer used AES-CBC due to its vulnerability in bit-flipping attacks.  
Here is a comprehensive guide of how to [crack AES-CBC](https://zhangzeyu2001.medium.com/attacking-cbc-mode-bit-flipping-7e0a1c185511).

## Enforcing secure passwords {#enforcing-secure-passwords}

Always assume the user is stupid, and it is your job to make sure that data that needs to be secured is secured with a strong password. You can estimate a password’s strength by calculating its [Entropy](https://proton.me/blog/what-is-password-entropy). Of course, in cases where security is absolutely necessary, pre-generated random passwords take away the headache of manually setting policies.

#### Keycloak {#keycloak-1}

Keycloak allows you to set password policies. Refer to the [guide](https://wjw465150.gitbooks.io/keycloak-documentation/content/server_admin/topics/authentication/password-policies.html) on how to set password policies. Ensure the password policy forces a strong password.

#### Manual Comparison {#manual-comparison}

If you ever need to manually implement password login, make sure the language comes with proper password handling. An indication on password strength or requirements can also help remind users to generate a strong password.

A simple “==” is vulnerable to [timing attacks](https://www.twingate.com/blog/glossary/timing%20attack). Thankfully, timing attacks are very easy to secure against using [constant time algorithms](https://medium.com/@ajay.monga73/timing-secrets-exploiting-returns-password-vulnerabilities-and-fix-in-java-d41ed95f8272). Realistically, even network jitter can make this attack a lot less feasible but it is not a reliable way of securing passwords.

## Serialising user input {#serialising-user-input}

Never assume the user input is what you want it to be. Strings and images uploaded by the user must be serialised. Here’s a recent example: [Cloudflare pending\_delete bug](https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-outage-february-20-2026/)

Example of not validating user input:

| if request.file\_path.lower().endswith('.jpg') or request.file\_path.lower().endswith('.jpeg'):           content\_type \= "image/jpeg"       elif request.file\_path.lower().endswith('.png'):           content\_type \= "image/png"       elif request.file\_path.lower().endswith('.jgw'):           content\_type \= "text/plain" |
| :---- |

In this case, the image can be simply validated with

| from PIL import Imagedef is\_valid\_image\_pillow(file\_name):    try:        with Image.open(file\_name) as img:            img.verify()            return True    except (IOError, SyntaxError):        return False |
| :---- |

### **Summary Of The Differences Between Prod And Dev** {#summary-of-the-differences-between-prod-and-dev}

For convenience sake here’s a summary of the differences you have to keep in mind

* SSL is mandatory for Keycloak (need to mount)

* Inspect element cannot be used in production  
* You cannot manually use a script in production after deploying the app

## Helm Charts {#helm-charts}

All necessary information can be found on the [documentation](https://helm.sh/docs/topics/charts/)

### Why use Helm Charts? {#why-use-helm-charts?}

In deployment, code runs in “pods”, which are isolated containers that cannot access the host OS. Helm charts can be used to pass environment variables and mount files so that your code is able to be configured.

Folder Structure:  
helm/  
├── Chart.yaml  
├── values.yaml  
└── templates/  
    ├── deployment.yaml  
    ├── service.yaml  
    ├── configmap.yaml  
    └── secret.yaml

### Introduction {#introduction-3}

The default helm chart can be created using the command `` `helm create <app-name>` ``, which also generates the default helm charts.

Helm charts are required for the whole app, as well as the individual services that you run. Before viewing some example helm charts, we need to look at the syntax of it so we can get a better understanding of what is going on.

Helm charts follow a yaml syntax, that is to say:

| key: valuekey2:   \- subKey1: value1   \- subKey2: value2 |
| :---- |

**\*\* NOTE: INDENTATION MATTERS IN A YAML FILE**

An additional feature of helm charts is that you can refer to values from other files. To do this, the variable is denoted with double curly branches ‘{{}}’ with the path to the value inside the curly braces.

| ports:   \- port: {{ .Values.service.port }} |
| :---- |

In this example, the value of ‘port’ points to the value.yaml file with key ‘service’ and subkey ‘port’.

Additionally, you can specify the specific indentation of helm chart values using a \``` nindent <number>` `` specifier, where each indentation is an increment of 2, such as: 

| labels:   {{- include "app-backend.labels" . | nindent 2 }} |
| :---- |

### Quick Start {#quick-start}

#### Chart.yaml {#chart.yaml}

The Chart.yaml from the documentation provides a comprehensive list of keywords, but the example below provides the minimum requirements. 

**NOTE: YOU CAN DEPRECATE CHART.YAML**

| apiVersion: v1name: \<my-chart\>version: 0.1.0appVersion: "0.1.0" description: Umbrella Helm chart for \<my-app\> full-stack applicationtype: applicationhome: [https://example.com](https://example.com)dependencies: \# Backend chart \- name: app-backend   version: "0.1.0"   repository: "file://charts/backend"   condition: backend.enabled \# Frontend chart \- name: app-frontend   version: "0.1.0"   repository: "file://charts/frontend"   condition: frontend.enabledmaintainers: \# (optional)  \- name: Tan    email: sample@example.comdeprecated: false |
| :---- |

`apiVersion`: depends on the specific helm version required; if the app requires at least Helm 3.0, can change to \`v2\`

`version: version number should follow Semantic Versioning naming scheme`

`dependencies/repository`: points towards the `Chart.yaml` of each container. In the example given, it points to the frontend and backend pods

#### value.yaml {#value.yaml}

The value.yaml file is paired with template/deployment.yaml for environment variables and volume mounting of secrets. It is never a standalone configuration but acts as shared variables across other yaml files.

A sample value.yaml keycloak configuration.

| keycloak:   volumeName: "keycloak-cert"   mountPath: "/etc/.secrets"   allowedGroups: "basic-user"   clientName: "app-client" |
| :---- |

##### deployment.yaml {#deployment.yaml}

The above value.yaml merely determines the shared variable names and values, but does not pass it into the application. To pass a variable into your application as an environment variable, a separate deployment.yaml is required. The deployment.yaml file is container specific, and a deployment.yaml file can only be for a single container.

However, we cannot start writing the deployment.yaml file without the base necessary configurations.

| apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata: name: {{ include "my-app.fullname" . }} labels:   {{- include "app-backend.labels" . | nindent 4 }}spec: replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} selector:   matchLabels:     {{- include "app-backend.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }} template:   metadata:     labels:       {{- include "app-backend.selectorLabels" . | nindent 8 }}   spec:     {{- with .Values.imagePullSecrets }}     imagePullSecrets:       {{- toYaml . | nindent 8 }}     {{- end }}     securityContext:       runAsNonRoot: true |
| :---- |

After laying out the foundation of the deployment.yaml, we can load the variables from values.yaml into the container as environment variables or a volume.

###### *Environment variable* {#environment-variable}

Environment variables are used where configurations need to be made in the container, without directly changing the code every time the environment changes. In the given example, the deployment.yaml file is configured for a generic pod, and the corresponding value.yaml file

| spec: template:   spec:     containers:       \- name: {{ .Chart.Name }}         image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"         imagePullPolicy: {{ .Values.image.pullPolicy }}         env:           \# Keycloak           \- name: KEYCLOAK\_CLIENT             value: {{ .Values.keycloak.clientName }} |
| :---- |

##### configmap.yaml {#configmap.yaml}

### How to mount secrets {#how-to-mount-secrets}

You can refer to a guide from the OpenShift website for examples: [A more secure way to handle secrets in OpenShift](https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2025/10/01/secure-way-handle-secrets-openshift#).

### 1\. Generate the secrets {#1.-generate-the-secrets}

You can use the OpenShift webUI to directly create a secret with the key and value, or load it using [secret.yaml](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/3.11/html/developer_guide/dev-guide-secrets). 

### 2\. Load the secrets into a volume {#2.-load-the-secrets-into-a-volume}

| volumes:\- name: {{ .Values.s3.volumeName }}  secret:  secretName: {{ .Values.s3.genericSecretName }}  items:    \- key: \<name-of-secret\>      path: app.crt |
| :---- |

You can use references to value.yaml for easier configuration and clearer mounts.

### 3\. Mount the cert into container {#3.-mount-the-cert-into-container}

| volumeMounts:\- name: {{ .Values.s3.volumeName }}  mountPath: {{ .Values.s3.mountPath }}  readOnly: true |
| :---- |

Setting the file to read only prevents accidental overwriting of file contents.

### 4\. Pass mount point as environment variable {#4.-pass-mount-point-as-environment-variable}

| name: \<env-variable-name\>  value: {{ .Values.s3.mountPath }}/app.crt |
| :---- |

Now, you successfully mounted your secret as a volume in the pod\! Your code will now be able to access the file path of your secret using `env-variable-name`.

# Roadmap

**Developer Onboarding Guide**

Standard Web Application Tech Stack

*Architecture · Tech Stack · Learning Roadmap*

# **Contents**

# **1\. Overview**

This guide covers the standard tech stack, system architecture, and a structured learning roadmap for developers joining the team. The stack is curated for seamless integration with the production environment and prioritises maintainability, readability, and ease of onboarding over raw performance.

Languages such as Rust or Go may offer superior speed, but come with a steeper learning curve that is rarely justified at our scale. The choices below reflect developer ergonomics appropriate for our user base and project size.

## **Quick Reference**

| Layer | Technology | Layer | Technology |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Backend** | Python / FastAPI | **Auth** | Keycloak |
| **Frontend** | TypeScript / React | **Database** | PostgreSQL |
| **ORM** | SQLAlchemy \+ Alembic | **Object Storage** | S3 / FlashBlade / MinIO |
| **HTTP Client** | Axios \+ TanStack Query | **Infra** | OpenShift, Helm, ArgoCD |
| **Testing** | pytest \+ Vitest | **Security** | Trivy \+ SonarQube |

# **2\. Architecture**

The diagram below describes the recommended system layout. Components outside the dotted boundary are managed production services — they are not owned or deployed by your team.

## **2.1 System Layers**

| APPLICATION LAYER  (your code) |
| ----- |
|  **Frontend** TypeScript · React · Vite ShadCN · TailwindCSS · Axios · TanStack Query *Keycloak-js (login & token retrieval only)* **Backend** Python 3.13 · FastAPI · Uvicorn · Pydantic SQLAlchemy 2.x · Alembic · psycopg · Boto3 python-keycloak · pytest · logging  |
| *▼  API requests \+ Keycloak token  ▼  Admin API  ▼  SQLAlchemy queries  ▼  Boto3 calls* |
| ***MANAGED SERVICES  (not owned by your team)*** |
|  **Keycloak** Authentication & authorisation Token issuance · SSO · RBAC **PostgreSQL** Relational database All app data · Schema via Alembic **S3 / Object Storage** FlashBlade / MinIO Files · Presigned URL access  |

## **2.2 Key Architectural Rules**

The following rules define where logic lives. Violating them leads to security issues, hard-to-test code, and maintenance problems.

| Backend only | Source of truth for all application data All business logic, permission checks, and state transitions Sole reader/writer of the database via SQLAlchemy Sole modifier of object storage via Boto3 Sole administrator of Keycloak (confidential client, Admin API) All API endpoints must validate the Keycloak token before processing |
| :---- | :---- |

| Frontend only | Presents UI and collects user input Sends requests to backend with Keycloak token attached UI-only validation (required fields, input formatting, basic feedback) Reads object storage via presigned GET URLs only — no direct writes Interacts with Keycloak only for login and token retrieval (keycloak-js) |
| :---- | :---- |

Note: Local development uses local versions of managed services (no SSL certs needed). Production requires SSL — missing certs will cause errors.

| :---- | :---- |

| :---- | :---- |

| CI/CD GitHub Actions \+ ArgoCD | github-actions  argocd  — build → scan → deploy pipeline |
| :---- | :---- |

| Security Scans Trivy \+ SonarQube | trivy  sonarqube  sonar-lint  — container and code scanning |
| :---- | :---- |

| Code Quality Black \+ Flake8 \+ ESLint \+ Prettier | black  flake8  eslint  prettier  — auto-format on save |
| :---- | :---- |

# **4\. Learning Roadmap**

The roadmap is structured in five phases. Complete each phase before moving to the next. Estimated durations are for trainees with some programming background \- adjust based on experience.

| Phase 1  Foundations    \~1–2 weeks |  |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Key tools & libraries** Python 3.13 \+ venv \+ pip TypeScript \+ Node.js basics VS Code \+ extensions CSS HTML DOM  | **Learning objectives** Create and activate a venv; install packages with pip Understand TypeScript types, interfaces, and basic generics Configure VS Code with Pylance, ESLint, Prettier, and SonarLint Learn the basics of the fundamental elements of the web  |

| Phase 2  Backend Core    \~2–3 weeks |  |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Key tools & libraries** FastAPI \+ Uvicorn Pydantic models SQLAlchemy 2.x ORM psycopg v3 Alembic migrations | **Learning objectives** Build and document REST endpoints with FastAPI Define Pydantic request/response schemas and validate data Create SQLAlchemy models and run queries Write and apply an Alembic migration against a local Postgres Add structured logging and error handling to a route |

| Phase 3  Frontend Core    \~2–3 weeks |  |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Key tools & libraries** React 19 \+ Vite TailwindCSS v4 ShadCN components React Router TanStack Query \+ Axios | **Learning objectives** Scaffold a Vite \+ React \+ TypeScript project Build pages with ShadCN components styled via Tailwind Implement client-side routing between pages with React Router Fetch, cache, and display data from the backend using TanStack Query Handle loading, error, and empty states in the UI |

| Phase 4  Integration — Auth, Storage & Testing    \~2 weeks |  |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Key tools & libraries** Keycloak-js (frontend) python-keycloak (backend) Boto3 \+ S3/MinIO pytest \+ unittest.mock Vitest | **Learning objectives** Protect frontend routes with keycloak-js token refresh Validate Keycloak tokens on FastAPI endpoints Upload and retrieve files via Boto3; serve via presigned URLs Write backend unit tests mocking the database and S3 client Write frontend component tests with Vitest |

| Phase 5  Infrastructure & DevOps (This is probably not happening)    \~1–2 weeks |  |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Key tools & libraries** OpenShift CLI (oc) Helm charts ArgoCD GitHub Actions Trivy \+ SonarQube | **Learning objectives** Deploy a containerised app to an OpenShift namespace Package the app with a Helm chart and customise values Connect a Git repo to ArgoCD for GitOps deployment Read a GitHub Actions pipeline and understand each step Interpret Trivy container scan and SonarQube code quality results |

## **4.1 Roadmap Summary**

| Phase | Focus | Duration | Key outcome |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Foundations | 1–2 weeks | Working local dev environment |
| 2 | Backend Core | 2–3 weeks | Functional FastAPI \+ DB service |
| 3 | Frontend Core | 2–3 weeks | Functional React SPA fetching real data |
| 4 | Integration | 2 weeks | Secured, tested, full-stack app |
| 5 | Infrastructure | 1–2 weeks | App deployed on OpenShift via ArgoCD |
